Live injury updates

The Seattle Seahawks could have their No. 1 quarterback on Sunday when they take on the Washington Commanders. Sam Darnold, who suffered a glute injury during the opening game of the season, was back at practice on Thursday as a full participant.

In Darnold's absence, Drew Lock threw for 187 yards and a touchdown during Seattle's Week 1 win over the New England Patriots. He followed that up during last week's win over the Arizona Cardinals with 235 passing yards and three touchdowns.

Head coach Mike Macdonald said Darnold is "on a good track right now" to play in Week 3 and the team will likely make a final decision sometime on Friday about whether he will start.

It's not looking good for Caleb Williams to be available for the Chicago Bears when they play the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night. The quarterback left Week 2 with a hamstring injury and, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, is not expected to be available. That would mean the next man up is Tyson Bagent, but he suffered a concussion in practice this week, which could lead to Case Keenum being under center.

Other Week 3 injuries to monitor:

  • Saquon Barkley suffered a stinger in Week 2, but after positive MRI results he returned to practice with the Eagles on Thursday. He was listed as a limited participant, so the door remains open for him to play against the Bears.

  • The Washington Commanders and Jayden Daniels got good news with the quarterback not requiring surgery on his injured elbow. General manager Adam Peters said Friday that an operation is "not on the table" and that they have not talked about placing Daniels on injured reserve, which would rule him out for at least four weeks.

  • Nico Collins of the Houston Texans and Zay Flowers of the Baltimore Ravens both missed Week 2 with injuries and bothremained out of practice this week. Collins and Flowers suffered hamstring injuries in Week 1. The Texans are set to travel to Indianapolis to face the Colts, while the Ravens are heading to Rio de Janeiro to face the Cowboys.

  • Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua remained out of practice after head coach Sean McVay said he was "not making great progress" with the hip/groin issue that kept him out of Week 2. What Nacua is dealing with now is not related to the psoas issue that caused him to miss time during training camp.

  • After being ruled out for the season with a knee injury, New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart will undergo surgery on Friday to repair his meniscus. According to The Athletic's Dan Duggan, Dart also suffered damage to his MCL and PCL, which will be addressed if needed. He is looking at a four-to-six month recovery period.

item.title: Miami Dolphins review: 5 Things I Think I Think About Week 2
item.description: The Dolphins are exactly who we thought they were. Maybe that’s not necessarily a bad thing.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 made me think, “OK, we lost, but maybe we’ll be better than people think.” Week 2 ground that idea into dust and already has me regretting my six-win prediction. Here’s my perhaps less-than-sanguine take on our team after Week 2.

Not all of the Dolphins’ problems are due to youth.

Do you remember the Takes No Talent wall from 2019? When Brian Flores coached the team, players (and coaches!) would have to run to the TNT wall following a mistake or lapse in execution. It was intended to emphasize effort, discipline and accountability.

I might not be the biggest Flores fan, but it takes no talent to:

  • Secure the snap before punting.
  • Make routine kicks.
  • Avoid procedural penalties.
  • Line up correctly.
  • Execute assignments.
  • Catch a punt.

This roster’s path to victory is already narrow due to its youth and dead cap allotment. They can’t be missing field goals, muffing punts, gifting opponents short fields and coming away empty on red-zone drives. The Dolphins aren’t good enough to beat themselves and their opponent on the same Sunday.

The lack of a pass rush might be the biggest problem on the roster.

When you strip a team down to the studs and start building from scratch, you can’t be surprised that none of your position rooms is giving you even league-average play. But the Dolphins’ pass rush has been exceptionally bad through the first two games. How bad?

  • The Dolphins are the only team to not record a sack through two games this season.
  • They also have the second-worst defensive passing rating allowed. Brock Purdy completed 91% of his passes on Sunday – 91%!
  • Sunday’s pressure statistics were just as bad. Fifty-seven pass rushes by tackles Zeek Biggers, Zach Sieler, Jordan Phillips and Keith Cooper generated just one quarterback pressure. On the edge, Josh Uche managed three pressures, but Malik Herring, Clelin Ferrell, Robert Beal, and Max Llewellyn failed to generate a single pressure on 25 combined pass-rushing snaps.

Part of their struggles could be attributed to draft strategy – remember the Dolphins passed on Reuben Bain to draft OL Kadyn Proctor. But something tells me even Bain wouldn’t be enough to fix this motley group.

My opinion of Austin Jackson is changing … for the better.

Don’t get me wrong – my opinion of AJ’s game wasn’t especially high. And Sunday’s game was epically bad:

  • 9 pressures allowed.
  • 2 sacks allowed.
  • 14% pressure rate allowed, which is the highest pressure percentage among qualifying offensive tackles.
  • False starts and holding penalties.

For one, that’s going to happen when you’re facing Maxx Crosby and Nick Bosa. Both are All-Pro-caliber pass rushers.

More to the point, Austin Jackson is on a one-year contract and is highly unlikely to be on the team next year. I’m not judging him by sacks or pressures allowed as much as I’m asking, “Can he hold down the fort at right tackle while Kadyn Proctor learns to play left guard?” In a rebuilding year, that’s all I want from AJ: Keep Malik Willis upright while Proctor develops into, hopefully, an All-Pro of his own. (And just stop with the calls to start Caedan Wallace. Wallace is a 26-year-old who has appeared in 10 games for his career. Wallace protecting Willis from Crosby or Bosa would have gotten Willis killed.) Maybe Proctor’s future is at right tackle, but let’s get him comfortable at guard before having that conversation.

Jeff Hafley’s job is safe for 2026.

Losing to the bad teams and getting blown out by the good teams is not a recipe for long-term job security, even for first-time coaches conducting a rebuild. Still, as we discussed earlier, this isn’t a year to be judged by wins and losses. Hafley is building a culture on a team where one-third of his roster comprises first- or second-year players. I believe he could go 0-17 and still be given another year to see this rebuild through.

What could make me change my mind? This:

Undisciplined play, mental errors, a broken locker room – those things might cause me to question if Jeff Hafley is the right person for the job. But if we continue to see players playing hard and first- and second-year players grow into their positions, I think he stays.

Rooting for the Dolphins will feel different this year.

I’m the last person to tell anyone how to fan, especially if you support the Dolphins. If you are 25 years old or younger, then you were not even alive the last time the team won a playoff game. The fact that people are willing to root for this team at all is astounding, if you stop to think about it.

We all knew the plan this offseason: Invest in youth and eat a record amount of dead cap. Still, hope springs eternal, especially in the final days before Labor Day. “Maybe if Malik is the second coming of Lamar Jackson, and if Players X and Y take a leap, who knows?” But after watching a couple of games, I think we have a better idea of what we’re in for. This isn’t one of those seasons where you think “Maybe we’ll steal a game from the Bills.” It’s more a season of “Maybe we’ll steal a game from the Jets,” and man, that’s hard to swallow.

And yet, despite all of it, I’m as excited about the long-term future of this team as I’ve been in years. After years of treading water, firing the GM but keeping the coach and then firing the coach but keeping the GM, we finally get to watch a team build from the ground up. A young, tough team that is fun to root for. We have a player who is 6’5”, 315 pounds, whose last name is literally “Biggers.” Are you kidding me? How can you not root for Zeek Biggers?

So fine, we’re underdogs against the Chiefs, like we’ll likely be throughout the season. But as these players grow, you can finally see a path toward the kind of sustained success this franchise hasn’t had in decades. You can sign me up for that right now.

item.title: The Packers' struggles could be the Jets' gain
item.description: As the football-following world began to come to terms with the possibility that the Packers could be very bad this year, Cowboys fans began to perk up.
item.content:encoded:
As the football-following world began to come to terms with the possibility that the Packers could be very bad this year, Cowboys fans began to perk up.

Thanks to the Micah Parsons trade, the Cowboys hold Green Bay's first-round pick in 2027. So, the worse the Packers do, the higher the 2027 first-round pick climbs.

But there's an important caveat, which works to the benefit of the New York Jets.

The trade that sent defensive tackle Quinnen Williams to Dallas includes an important term as to the 2027 first-round pick the Jets received. It's not necessarily the Cowboys' pick. It's the higher of the two picks the Cowboys will have.

Which means that, if the Packers bottom out (and the Cowboys don't), the Jets get the Green Bay first-round pick in 2027.

The Jets, of course, failed to help themselves on Sunday, when they blew a 10-point lead to the Packers and mismanaged the late-game and overtime scenarios.

Still, it's good news for the Jets. Especially since they also hold the Colts' first-round pick for 2027 — and the Colts are 0-2.

item.title: The Packers stink, and Tucker Kraft yelling at fans only makes it more embarrassing
item.description: Tucker Kraft blames Packers fans for boos during Falcons loss: 'It's not going to help us win'
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Falcons were in a dark place heading into their Week 3 matchup against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field. The Falcons were already 0-2, outscored 54-16 across their first two games, and coming off an embarrassing loss to the Carolina Panthers last Sunday that inspired my colleague James Dator to write the artful headline “The Falcons suck so bad they’ve reached new levels of suck.”

The Falcons were getting their quarterback back for Week 3, with Michael Penix mercifully making his season debut after a couple of Cooper Rush disasterclasses to start the year. Still, the Packers were -4.5 or -5.5 in most major sportsbooks to win the game, mostly because that’s how bad Atlanta had been to begin the season.

The Falcons beat the Packers 35-14 in a loss that should send Green Bay spiraling while uplifting the spirits of Atlanta fans who thought the season might already be over. The Falcons dominated after the first quarter with superstars Bijan Robinson (194 yards and two touchdowns on the ground) and Drake London (194 yards receiving) both crushing the Green Bay defense while Penix made some nice throws and managed the game effectively. This result feels like it’s more about Green Bay than the Falcons, though.

The Packers’ performance was so pathetic that the home fans let them hear it. Lambeau Field booed the Packers during the fourth quarter, there were even scant “ATL” chants being heard in the stands. After the game, Green Bay tight end Tucker Kraft chastised the fans who booed the home players. This whole quote is a big yikes.

Here are the full comments from Kraft after the game. Again: yikes!

“That’s pretty tough. Like everyone pictures Lambeau Field and not boos. I don’t picture boos. I picture my home stadium. That’s tough. It’s pretty disappointing, especially for a home opener. It’s pretty disappointing. It’s not going to help us win. Like I don’t know what people think that’s going to rally us or something like that. But that’s — we’re grown men. We’re mentally strong enough, capable enough to get back on the field and play ball. But it’d probably much easier with the 70,000 people behind us rather than opposing us.”

It’s hard to blame Packers fans for voicing their frustration after such a bad showing. This Green Bay fan in particular was really going through it:

Green Bay’s defense got run over all night, failing to force the Atlanta offense into a 3-and-out all night. QB Jordan Love was consistently under duress despite only being sacked once. Green Bay has no running game to speak of with Josh Jacobs held out due to domestic abuse charges. The Packers finished with 17 rushing yards on the night, while the Falcons finished with 249 rushing yards.

The Packers’ special teams was so bad that they gave up a blocked field goal to a team with only 10-men on the field:

The Packers have problems in all three phases of the game right now. This team could very easily be 0-3. After losing to Minnesota and Carson Wentz 39-22 in their opener, Green Bay needed a miracle just to sneak by the Jets in overtime in Week 2.

Green Bay’s roster just feels thin in the trenches, in the defensive backfield, and in the playmaking groups at running back and wide receiver. Head coach Matt LaFleur received a controversial extension this offseason, and that already feels like a catastrophe. LaFleur has a history of coaching scared, and it feels like it’s robbed this team of its confidence. Green Bay also doesn’t have its 2027 first-round pick, which was sent out in the Micah Parsons trade, and is now controlled by the New York Jets. Parsons remains out with a torn ACL, though he’s expected back by midseason.

The Packers stink out loud, and their players are embarrassing themselves with quotes like the one Kraft offered after the game. It’s totally possible the Packers just straight up suck, and they can’t even dream on their draft pick in a loaded 2027 class. Bringing back LaFleur was clearly a terrible idea.

Packers fans are saying this is the worst it has been in the last 30 years. It’s hard to argue. Any team capable of making the Falcons look that good obviously has big problems. It’s going to be a long season in Green Bay.

item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 9/25/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

To no surprise, Smitty is off to a strong start. Did anyone actually question if he could be WR1? That never shouldn’t been in doubt, if it even was at all.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

NFL wide receiver rankings: Jaxon Smith-Njigba leads top 32 – PFF

DeVonta Smith, Philadelphia Eagles. Smith has benefited from the departure of A.J. Brown this offseason, averaging 2.30 yards per route run and ranking fourth at the position with a 91.4 PFF receiving grade. Now the No. 1 target in Philadelphia, he has a strong chance to put together the best season of his career.

Eagles vs. Bears Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 3 enemy – BGN

4 – What’s the biggest matchup in the Bears’ favor and the biggest matchup against their favor? Well, I think the easiest one is the biggest disadvantage, and that will be the Eagles offensive line vs. the Bears defensive line. I understand Landon Dickerson is out, and the Eagles offensive line isn’t quite what it used to be, but it’s still a strong unit, and the Bears defensive line just isn’t. If the Philly OL can’t control the line of scrimmage, that would be rather surprising. I think the biggest advantage for them is the fact that the Eagles are struggling to stop the run right now, and the Bears block it extremely well. Maybe it’s a cliché, but I think this game is going to come down to controlling the line of scrimmage. Both teams have strong offensive lines and have a chance to control the line when they have the ball. I think the Bears need to really have long drives and keep their defense off the field. Can they do it without Caleb Williams? We will see on Monday night.

Eagles mailbag: OL talk galore: Regrets? Trades? Reason for hope? – PhillyVoice

Question from @jjapostolico (via Bluesky): Do Jurgens’ and Dickerson’s health make them less viable than the young guys like Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin? Dickerson has been a great player for the last half decade for the Eagles. He was a first-round talent who they got in Round 2 because he had major injury concerns. I think that when they drafted him they knew he wasn’t going to have some sort of 12-year career, and they got a bunch of Pro Bowl seasons out of him. But it does feel like the end is near, and we could kind of see it in training camp, even before he performed poorly Week 1 against the Commanders. The younger guys are more viable options than him at this point. Jurgens has kind of gotten lumped in with Dickerson because he had injury issues all last season and both guys went to Colombia for stem cell treatments during the offseason. But to me, Jurgens looked fine in training camp, at least compared to Dickerson. In Week 1, Jurgens had a couple of penalties in the first quarter, but I thought he played well enough otherwise. Obviously, he had a terrible game Week 2 against Simmons after he was forced into a new role. But I’m not yet ready to say that he’s a candidate for replacement in the starting lineup.

Week 3 NFL game preview: Chicago Bears vs. Philadelphia Eagles – Windy City Gridiron

The first primetime game for the 2026 Chicago Bears has lost much of its luster since the team will most likely be starting its third quarterback on Monday night. The Bears welcome the Philadelphia Eagles to Soldier Field in what should have been a great matchup of historical franchises with young quarterbacks dueling it out. But the NFL is a fickle thing. Bears head coach Ben Johnson has to navigate his first game without his QB1 or QB2. And the Eagles, coming in 2-0 but not looking dominant, have a lot to prove. Beyond wanting to flush the memories of Black Friday last season, when the Bears completely dominated them. The Eagles want to make a statement that they’re back to being true contenders and that their new offense is working well. Even with a third QB, it should be an interesting game. Let’s get into the opponent then.

One thing we’ve learned about the Eagles at every position group through two weeks: Offense edition – PHLY Eagles

Tight end: Howie Roseman’s view of the position needs to evolve. I wonder, if given truth serum as he often likes to say, if the tight end position is the group Howie Roseman would most like a mulligan on from this offseason. For as much credit as Roseman should get for rebuilding the Eagles receiving corps in a post-A.J. Brown world, there are as many if not more questions about whether his additions at tight end are sufficient for the offense Mannion wants to run. At the start of the offseason, Roseman said he needed to change the way he viewed the position to better reflect the value of versatility on the perimeter rather than prioritizing capable pass-catching options, something that has accelerated league-wide even further this season. According to TruMedia, the Rams, Bills, Bears, and Ravens have all run more plays out of 13 personnel through two weeks than any team did this time last season. The Rams and Bills in particular have double the snaps with three tight ends on the field this year than last year’s leader (the Arizona Cardinals with 20 snaps). Watching these teams, it’s not hard to understand why they’ve shifted toward getting heavier personnel sets on the field. It often forces modern defenses set up to play with five defensive backs to instead play out of their base personnel groupings with one fewer and gives the offense an advantage on outside-zone runs in particular because of the improved blocking on the outside. And for teams like the Rams and Bills, the versatility of their tight-end rooms allows them to still throw out of those looks without sacrificing too much of a threat downfield. According to TruMedia, the Bills have generated four explosive plays out of 13-personnel this season, more than a handful of offenses have managed overall this season. At least through two weeks, the Eagles tight end room seems behind the curve. Eli Stowers projected as a receiving-only tight end even before a disappointing summer ended with a quad strain that landed him on injured reserve. Johnny Mundt’s addition gave them the option to put two trusted blocking options on the field to start the season, but Mundt’s even struggled at times in understandably difficult matchups with bigger defensive linemen. With Dallas Goedert sidelined and Zach Ertz stepping into his role, the room is not tailor-made for this outside zone-based system Mannion wants to run. It may be one of Roseman’s biggest misses this offseason, especially considering the questions about Stowers’ usage will likely extend beyond just his rookie season.

Why Jalen Hurts got emotional pulling up to Nissan Stadium in Nashville Sunday – NBCSP

Hurts, in his weekly chat with the Eagles beat writers after practice, grew emotional sharing a story about the Eagles’ team bus pulling up to Nissan Stadium in Nashville Sunday before the Eagles-Titans game and how a giant photo of long-time Titans quarterback Steve McNair on the side of the stadium caught his attention. “It was a really good feeling and a bit emotional feeling, you know, pulling up to the stadium and seeing Steve McNair on the wallpaper outside,” Hurts said. “He’s the only one that I’ve looked up to … I got to meet, you know, M.J. (Michael Jordan) and, you know, build relationships with him and Tom Brady and all these other guys. Steve McNair is the only one that I’ve truly looked up to and watched and been enamored by and never got to meet him. So I think that was special for that reason. I was reminded of that when we pulled up to the stadium and it kind of hit me there.”

The Best Bets of NFL Week 3 – The Ringer

Philadelphia Eagles at Chicago Bears (+4.5). If Tyson Bagent is able to play, the Bears catching more than a field goal is a bet for me. Case Keenum has not played in an NFL game since 2023. The Eagles have real questions through the middle of the defense that have made them look susceptible to the run in the first two weeks. Philly ranks in the bottom third in EPA per rush after games against Washington and Tennessee. That should raise some flags. The Eagles offense has been reliant on Jalen Hurts throwing the ball on third-and-long because the early-down run game is nonexistent through two weeks. Great spot for Chicago at home as an underdog, but I just cannot bet Keenum here.

Zach Ertz: I never wanted to leave Philadelphia, glad to be back to my favorite place – PFT

Veteran tight end Zach Ertz has returned to Philadelphia for his second stint with the Eagles, and he says he never wanted to leave. Ertz, who was drafted by the Eagles in 2013 and traded to the Cardinals in 2021, said he never knew if the Eagles would welcome him back, but always hoped they would. “There was never a plan to come back,” Ertz said. “I never wanted to leave in the first place, so let’s just put that out there. The opportunity finally arose where I could come back. There’s been times I asked in the past to come back and it didn’t come to fruition for whatever reason. But for me, it’s just a blessing to be back.”

NFL Fantasy 2026 Start ‘Em, Sit ‘Em: Wide receivers for Week 3 – NFL.com

SIT — Despite running the most routes among Bears wide receivers through two games, Rome Odunze has just five catches on seven targets. And while his average of 19 yards per reception is impressively high, Odunze’s not seeing the target rate we expect from WR1s … or WR2s … or WR3s. To make matters worse, Caleb Williams just suffered a hamstring injury. And to make worse matters even worse, the Eagles have been extremely tough against outside wide receivers. This could be the Luther Burden III breakout game, but Odunze should NOT crack starting lineups in Week 3.

Zack Baun Mic’d Up in INSANE last-minute win at Titans – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

All-Pro linebacker. All-Pro teammate. Zack Baun was Mic’d Up for the frenetic last-minute victory over the Tennessee Titans. The Bald Eagle was fired up on the game-winning drive.

NY Giants will ride with Jameis Winston at quarterback, as they should – Big Blue View

I keep seeing the opinion that if the Giants’ season turns into a train wreck, and they end up with the opportunity to draft Arch Manning, Dante Moore, Trinidad Chambliss or another top 10-worthy quarterback they should do it. My view is that idea is nonsense. One knee injury and two games missed because of a concussion doesn’t mean it is time to give up on the idea that Dart can and will be a top-tier NFL quarterback. Drafting over Dart, and starting over, is foolishness. What I could sign off on is the idea of drafting a young player in the middle rounds and trying to develop him as a viable backup. That doesn’t always work, but investing a fourth- or fifth-round pick is not that big of a gamble. I don’t know who the first one to point this out was, but I did see it online and it is correct. Matthew Stafford, who is heading to the Hall of Fame, was limited by injuries to just 13 games over his first two seasons. That was way back in 2009 and 2010, and he’s done OK since then.

Cowboys injuries: P.J. Locke, Cobie Durant DNP – Blogging The Boys

For the Cowboys, Cobie Durant (hamstring) did not practice. Also not practicing with the team were P.J. Locke (foot), DeMarvion Overshown (hamstring), and Malik Hooker (forearm). All seem unlikely to play with two DNPs to open the week. On Thursday, the Ravens were still without receiver Zay Flowers (hamstring) and offensive lineman Ronnie Stanley (toe). Flowers is a big part of the Baltimore offense and is a dynamic weapon the team relies upon at multiple levels in the field in a variety of offensive looks.

Commanders vs. Seahawks Thursday injury report: Javon Kinlaw returns – Hogs Haven

The Commanders got a little piece of good news in a sea of bad injury luck on Thursday, as defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw returned to practice in a limited capacity. That’s a win for Washington, as Kinlaw’s off to a solid start this season. He’s dealing with back and shoulder issues, according to the Commanders participation report. They’re still working without some important players, with linebacker Frankie Luvu (groin), tight end Chig Okonkwo (hamstring), right guard Sam Cosmi (concussion), safety Nick Cross (illness) and, of course, quarterback Jayden Daniels (elbow).

Commanders GM: Elbow surgery ‘not on table’ for QB Daniels – ESPN

Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels won’t undergo surgery on his dislocated left elbow and, as of now, he won’t be placed on injured reserve according to general manager Adam Peters. Daniels spent the past three days visiting specialists who examined his elbow. Throughout the process, one source close to the situation said surgery was a last option. Peters confirmed that prognosis while appearing on his weekly paid radio appearance on 106.7 The Fan in Washington, D.C. “As of right now surgery is not on the table and we have not discussed IR,” Peters told The Junkies. If that holds true, then Daniels would return within four weeks; a stint on injured reserve would require him to miss four games. In the next three weeks Washington plays Seattle, Indianapolis and the Giants.

NFL Expert Picks for Week 3– SB Nation

The season rolls on to Week 3 and it’s unclear how much more we’ve learned about any of these teams. While the NFL is always unpredictable, this season feels especially chaotic with key injuries happening early, wild upsets reigning supreme, and Tyler Shough and Bryce Young being the Top 2 quarterbacks in the NFL … somehow. This week has some really chalk-y picks, and that’s okay. Nobody has any faith in the Chargers to beat the Bills, for good reason — same with the Lions over the Jets and Seahawks over Commanders. Two sneaky games on the schedule to watch in Week 3 is the wet noodle fight between the Titans and Giants (sans Jaxson Dart), as well as Ravens vs. Cowboys, which could be a banger.

item.title: Will the Chiefs’ offense see the best of Xavier Worthy soon?
item.description: Time is running out for Kansas City’s 2024 first-round pick to prove he’s a high-caliber weapon.
item.content:encoded:
I loved the pick. Unabashedly loved it.

“He’s fast, he’s productive, and he’s going to add the element this offense has been missing.”

That was my initial impression when the Kansas City Chiefs drafted wide receiver Xavier Worthy in the first round.

That was not necessarily the consensus. Some national analysts panned the selection because he was more of the same for the Chiefs’ receiver room, with too many small, gadget-type receivers. I rejected the notion. This would be different. Andy Reid selected him in the first round for a reason. He clearly had a plan.

That appeared to be the case, at least in year one. After a slow start — 20 receptions in his first 9 games — Worthy was thrust into action in the second half of his rookie year. He became the team’s leading receiver in the second half of the season after Rashee Rice went down to injury. Worthy racked up nearly 400 yards in his final seven regular-season games. That seemed to offer a glimpse of what was to come.

But then he ran into tight end Travis Kelce on a crossing route in the first game of the 2025 season, and everything changed. His shoulder became an issue. He missed a couple of games. An ankle injury also held him back. He finished the 2025 campaign with barely 500 receiving yards and only one touchdown.

It was a frustrating season, marred by injury.

The Chiefs spent the offseason telling anyone who would listen that this year would be different. Worthy would be healthy, and we would see a return to the player we watched in the second half of the 2024 campaign. I was optimistic. This would be the year he proved the doubters wrong, once and for all.

I’m still waiting for that to happen.

Worthy doesn’t look like the confident player he was in the second half of his rookie year. He’s shying away from contact. He’s not strong at the catch point. He’s not beating defenders to the corner. I’m struggling to understand how to use a player who doesn’t win deep, doesn’t play with the physicality needed to win across the middle, and can’t break tackles to win after the catch.

What’s the proper usage for such a wide receiver? That seems to be the question the Chiefs are asking, too. I hope the Chiefs find that answer sooner rather than later.

This offense looks like a legitimate contender. Running back Kenneth Walker has added an explosive element the Chiefs have been lacking for years. Quarterback Patrick Mahomes looks as confident as he has in his supporting cast since 2022. Kelce is rejuvenated. Wideout Tyquan Thornton is a legitimate deep threat. Receiver Rashee Rice is working his way back to prime form.

If Worthy can return to his second-half 2024 form, this group is cooking with gas.

Can he get back to that form, though? That remains to be seen. The history of first-round wide receivers who have produced like Worthy through two-plus seasons is less than ideal.

60 wide receivers were selected in the first round between 2011 & 2025. Worthy ranks 32nd among them in receptions, 38th in receiving yards and 33rd in receiving touchdowns through his first 33 games. By volume, none of those statistics are particularly alarming.

The efficiency is where the trends are far more worrisome.

Worthy is targeted at roughly the average rate among the 60 wide receivers selected in the first round over the past 15 years, but he’s produced fewer yards per target than nearly any other receiver on the list.

His 6.6 yards per target is through his first 33 career regular season games ranks 51st among that group. The only other first-round wide receivers over that stretch to average fewer than 7 yards per reception through 33 career regular season games are Kevin White, Garrett Wilson, Josh Doctson, A.J. Jenkins, Nelson Agholor, John Ross, Kadarius Toney, Jalen Reagor, Xavier Leggette, Breshad Perriman, Cordarreelle Patterson, Tavon Austin, N’Keal Harry, Laquon Treadwell, Corey Coleman and Jonathan Baldwin.

Uh oh.

That’s not a group you want to be included in. It’s a who’s who of wide receiver busts over the past decade-plus. It’s especially worrisome that Worthy is producing like this with a future Hall of Fame coach and quarterback. Most receivers who overcame poor early-career efficiency (Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Malik Nabers, and Garrett Wilson) were dealing with a poorly designed offensive scheme, a below-average quarterback situation, or both. That excuse or explanation doesn’t apply to Worthy.

The only reason I’m holding out hope my priors are correct on Worthy is the injuries. Maybe the first couple of weeks are a blip on the radar. Maybe he’ll have a second half similar to his rookie year. Maybe he’s still tentative after playing through so many ailments last season, and it’ll just take time to get himself right.

Maybe. Hopefully.

The Chiefs offense doesn’t need Worthy to step up the way it once did. But it sure would be nice if he could. I’m still holding out hope, but patience is running thin.

item.title: Saints vs. Raiders predictions: Bring the noise
item.description: Week 3 finds the Saints finally back home in the dome
item.content:encoded:
After opening the season with back-to-back road games, the New Orleans Saints finally return to Caesars Superdome on Sunday, looking to build on their first win of the season.

New Orleans enters Week 3 with a 1-1 record following a 24-17 victory over the Baltimore Ravens. Meanwhile, the Las Vegas Raiders arrive in New Orleans undefeated at 2-0 under first-year head coach and former Saints offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak.

Sunday’s matchup presents an opportunity for the Saints to build some early-season momentum, but it won’t come easy against a Raiders team that has gotten off to a strong start.

Through the first two weeks, Tyler Shough has given Saints fans plenty of reasons to be optimistic.

After throwing for 410 yards and three touchdowns in the season-opening overtime loss to Detroit, Shough followed up with another solid performance against Baltimore, completing 27 of 34 passes and scoring the go-ahead touchdown on the ground. His connection with wide receiver Chris Olave has already proven to be one of New Orleans’ biggest offensive weapons, and the Saints will need that chemistry again Sunday.

However, protecting Shough could be a major concern. With left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. out indefinitely with an ankle injury, New Orleans must find a way to contain Raiders defensive end Maxx Crosby, who is capable of disrupting an offense on his own.

One of the biggest storylines surrounding Sunday’s matchup is the return of Klint Kubiak, who served as the Saints’ offensive coordinator in 2024. Kubiak has led Las Vegas to a 2-0 start, with veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins leading an offense that has shown it can make big plays. Cousins threw three touchdown passes in the Raiders’ 26-14 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 2, while wide receiver Tre Tucker racked up 119 receiving yards.

New Orleans showed improvement defensively against Baltimore, particularly in the second half. The Saints will need another strong performance, especially when it comes to pressuring Cousins and preventing explosive plays.

The biggest difference this week is that New Orleans will have a very loud and proud home crowd behind them.

Prediction: Saints 34 – Raiders 27

You can expect this one to be another entertaining matchup, with both offenses finding ways to put points on the board. But finally playing in the dome for the first time this season will give the Saints an extra spark, and I think they will make enough plays in the fourth quarter to hand the Raiders their first loss of the season.

item.title: Seahawks vs. Commanders predictions: Expect another big game from Seattle’s rushing attack
item.description: Seattle’s rushing attack could be the key to another road win against Washington.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks enters Week 3 with a 2-0 record and will travel to Maryland to take on the Washington Commanders and try and extend their winning streak to 13 games. The Seahawks are currently 7.5-point favorites at FanDuel Sportsbook, with the total set at 40.5 points.

This matchup looks considerably different than it did when the lines first opened. Washington is 0-2 after losing 37-20 to Dallas and will be without Jayden Daniels, while Seattle is still waiting to determine whether Sam Darnold will return from his injury.

That uncertainty makes quarterback-specific bets less appealing for now. Instead, there are several other markets that stand out, particularly with Seattle’s rushing attack and its defense.

Here are four predictions for Seahawks-Commanders.

1. Jadarian Price scores a touchdown

Jadarian Price’s status is one of the things to monitor before kickoff, but if the rookie is active, I like his chances of finding the end zone. Price left Seattle’s 31-7 victory over Arizona with a chest injury, although his initial X-rays were negative. He was limited in practice, keeping the door open for him to play against Washington.

Price has already shown why Seattle invested a first-round pick in him. Price had 52 rushing yards on 10 carries against New England in Week 1 before adding 52 yards on 13 carries against Arizona, including a 25-yard run.

Prediction: Jadarian Price anytime touchdown scorer

2. Jaxon Smith-Njigba goes over 90 receiving yards

At this point, there isn’t much reason to stop expecting big numbers from Jaxon Smith-Njigba.

JSN has 17 receptions for 277 yards and four touchdowns through two games, including a three-touchdown performance against Arizona. He has quickly become the focal point of Seattle’s passing game, regardless of who is playing quarterback.

The bigger question is whether Washington can find a way to slow him down.

The Commanders enter this game after allowing 37 points to Dallas, while Seattle’s offense has already shown it can generate explosive plays through multiple areas of the field.

Seattle could also have opportunities to attack through the air if Washington commits extra defenders to stopping the run.

The one concern is game script. If Seattle controls the game early, there may not be enough passing volume for JSN to approach another 150-yard performance. Still, his role makes 90 yards a reasonable target.

Prediction: Jaxon Smith-Njigba over 90 receiving yards

3. Seahawks cover -7.5

The current FanDuel line has Seattle favored by 7.5 points.

That is a larger number than the Seahawks have had to cover in either of their first two games, but there are reasons to believe Seattle can create enough separation.

The Seahawks have outscored their opponents 44-17 through two games. The defense has been the team’s biggest constant, while the offense has found ways to produce despite the uncertainty at quarterback.

Washington, meanwhile, is 0-2 and will have to adjust to playing without Daniels. Marcus Mariota will take over at quarterback, changing the way the Commanders can attack Seattle’s defense.

The biggest concern with laying 7.5 points is Seattle’s offensive ceiling if the quarterback situation remains unsettled. But the Seahawks don’t necessarily need another 30-point performance to cover.

If Seattle establishes its rushing attack and controls the clock, a two-score victory is within reach.

Prediction: Seahawks -7.5

4. Under 40.5 total points

The total is currently set at 40.5 points at FanDuel.

This might seem strange after Seattle scored 31 points last week, but the Seahawks have yet to play a game that went over this number. Their defense has also allowed just 17 points through the first two weeks.

Washington has gone in the opposite direction, with both of its games going over the closing total. But the Commanders will now have to play without Daniels, potentially changing the way they approach the game offensively.

Without their starting quarterback, Washington could lean more heavily on the running game and shorter throws rather than asking Mariota to consistently attack downfield against Seattle’s defense.

Seattle could also become more run-heavy if it builds a lead, which would help shorten the game and reduce the number of possessions available to both teams. A game finishing somewhere in the 20s for Seattle and the 10s for Washington would comfortably stay below the current number.

Prediction: Under 40.5 points

Final score prediction

The biggest variable remains Seattle’s quarterback situation, but the Seahawks have enough talent around the position to make that uncertainty less important than it might appear.

Seattle should be able to establish its rushing attack against Washington, while its defense has the matchup to make life difficult for a Commanders offense without Daniels.

I expect Washington to keep things competitive early, but Seattle should pull away in the second half.

Seahawks 24, Commanders 13

That gives Seattle an 11-point victory, enough to cover the current 7.5-point spread while keeping the game below the 40.5-point total.

item.title: Bills rookie WR Skyler Bell is probably going to make his NFL debut vs. Chargers
item.description: It’s looking like we will see Bell for the first time in the regular season on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills are experiencing some receiver injuries ahead of Week 3’s game against the Chargers, but we can’t forget the team drafted a wideout in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft.

Skyler Bell has been a healthy scratch for the first two contests of the season after he worked his way back from an injury in the summer that kept him out of the first two preseason games in August.

In the final exhibition outing, draft pick from UConn led the team with seven snags for 49 yards and took a jet sweep 28 yards for a touchdown in Buffalo’s 28-27 win.

I’m ready to see Bell in a real game, aren’t you?

D.J. Moore was downgraded from limited Wednesday to DNP on Thursday. Keon Coleman has yet to practice this week.

When two receivers are DNP on Thursday during a week with a Sunday game, chances are another receiver is going to be called upon in the upcoming contest.

That’s why Bell is almost assuredly going to be running routes for the first time as a professional in Week 3 against a Chargers secondary that ranks 26th in EPA per drop back allowed through two games.

Regarding Bell the player, as a refresher, here’s what I wrote about him before the draft:

“Skyler Bell is a modern inside–outside wide receiver with a lighter, compact build and enough length through his limbs to play bigger than his listed size. He’s nimble and light on his feet, showing noticeable quickness off the line and smooth acceleration into his routes. Bell isn’t physically imposing, but he moves easily and fluidly, giving him the flexibility to align both in the slot and outside depending on matchup and usage.

From a skill standpoint, Bell wins with suddenness more than power. He shows clean footwork on underneath routes and has double moves in his bag thanks to his ability to change speeds and directions without gearing down. He’s a clear hands-catcher who consistently plucks the ball away from his frame, and despite his size, he’s a respectable contested-catch finisher due to strong tracking instincts rather than leaping ability or physical dominance. After the catch, Bell is functional but not dynamic — he won’t consistently break tackles, yet he has enough juking ability and spatial awareness to avoid clean hits and steal extra yards in space. Physical coverage gives him trouble early in routes, and his route running, while solid, doesn’t consistently uncover defenders with nuance alone. Speed is slightly above average, and concentration lapses show up at times with a few too many easy drops on film.

Bell projects as a rotational NFL receiver whose value comes from versatility, reliable hands mechanics, and functional route ability rather than any standout trait. There’s no glaring weakness in his profile, but also no defining calling card that elevates him beyond a complementary role at this stage. He profiles best as a WR3/WR4 option who can move around formations, contribute underneath, and win selectively in contested situations, but likely won’t tilt coverage or demand schemed touches.”

I had a late second/early third-round grade on him and compared him to Sterling Shepard.

Not only did they appear similar on the field, they were almost mirror images of each other with very comparable combine workouts.

Shepard was 5’10” and 194 pounds with 4.48 speed, a 41-inch vertical, and 128” broad jump all the way back in 2016. Bell measured in at 5’11 5/8” with 4.41 speed, a 41-inch vertical, and 133” broad jump. So Buffalo’s receiver is a little bigger with slightly more juice.

And the Bills offense has exuded juice through two games.

Josh Allen’s enormous arm is being accentuated by head coach Joe Brady. Don’t be surprised if Bell is thrown into the mix and targeted downfield in this one. To me, his best bet to get open against sizable veteran outside corners Tarheeb Still and Cam Hart, who have 4.52 and 4.50 speed respectively, is on vertical routes.

While the gadget plays haven’t been part of Buffalo’s offense through two games beyond a jet sweep to Moore, expect Bell to get schemed up on some high-percentage throws or even credited with a carry simply because of his speed and explosiveness. That’s a more sensible ask for a rookie in his NFL debut than hoping he gets open on his own underneath or at the intermediate level.

In Week 2, a huge opportunity was thrust upon Coleman, and he delivered with six catches for 63 yards, including four grabs that went for first downs.

Bell will likely get a few chances to demonstrate the burst, long speed, and edge that were all very apparent on film during his 101-catch, 1,278-yard, 13-touchdown final season in college last year.

item.title: Do you trust Tyson Bagent or Case Keenum more against the Eagles?
item.description: It doesn’t look like Caleb Williams is playing on MNF, so we ask you Bears fans, would it be better if Case Keenum or Tyson Bagent faced Vic Fangio’s defense?
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears have a big matchup on Monday Night Football, taking on the Philadelphia Eagles. If the Bears lose, they’ll fall below .500 for the first time in a year. It’s only game three, but obviously, everyone would like to see the Bears get back on track after a tough loss in week two against the Minnesota Vikings.

Caleb Williams was knocked out of the game, and Ben Johnson has said that he is week-to-week, but almost everyone is certain that he will miss the Eagles game. If he does, that means it will either be Tyson Bagent, if he can clear concussion protocol, or Case Keenum, the veteran QB who has been mostly considered an assistant QB coach in a Bears uniform.

Bagent has the youth; Keenum has the veteran experience (but is it too much experience, if you know what I mean).

Who do you trust more against the Eagles: Tyson Bagent or Case Keenum?

I think the easy answer without thinking would be Tyson Bagent. But this Eagles defense is led by the great Vic Fangio, and we know that Vic has the ability to put inexperienced QBs in a blender. Would the Bears be better off with Keenum, who happens to be 3-0 career against Fangio (albeit when he was much younger), who can read a defense as well as anybody in the league and make snap decisions with the football?

Answer: This one, for me, is really difficult to answer. I think the idea of Keenum makes a ton of sense to go up against the Eagles and Fangio. He is a statue back there, but he can stand and deliver. The question is, who is Case Keenum at this point? In the preseason, Keenum was outstanding (as he was in the 2025 preseason as well). Keenum was 25 of 40 for 354 yards, 2 TDs, and 0 INTs. That’s good enough for a 107.7 rating. However, we have to take into account that he was going up against 3rd-stringers.

Keenum hasn’t thrown a ball in the regular season since 2023, and in his final four years where he played (2020-2023), the numbers were poor. He threw just 140 attempts over those 4 years and had a yards-per-attempt average under 6. He also had as many INTs as TDs (4 each).

So we have to ask ourselves: with Keenum, are we getting the guy who can operate Ben Johnson’s system brilliantly in the preseason, or are we getting the washed QB that looked terrible in his last few regular-season games?

While I’ve been leaning towards Keenum for most of this week, I think, in the end, Bagent, if he can play, makes more sense. Bagent also operates Johnson’s system well in the preseason, and his arrow is pointing up, not down. If it’s Keenum, I don’t think it’s a huge difference. If we ranked QBs on a scale of 1 to 10 to face Philly and Caleb is a 10, I think Bagent is a 6 and Keenum is a 5.

I think the way Garrett Bradbury is playing with those Eagles DTs, I would rather have a more mobile QB in Bagent because I think the Bears will give up a little pressure. So while I will have almost as much confidence in Keenum as I would with Bagent, I think I lean just a little bit on the Bagent side.

What do you say, Bears fans? Would you rather see Bagent or Keenum out there against the Eagles? Sound off in the comments section!

item.title: Lions vs. Jets predictions: 4 keys to victory in Week 3
item.description: Predicting what the Detroit Lions will do to earn a victory over the New York Jets in Week 3 of the 2026 season.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions (1-1) and New York Jets (1-1) will square off in a Week 3 battle as coach Dan Campbell welcomes back his protégé, Aaron Glenn, to Ford Field for the first time since the former defensive coordinator left for the Big Apple.

“Our players know exactly what’s coming in here because the defensive coordinator was here for (four) years,” Campbell said of Glenn and the Jets. “Turn on the tape. … This is not going to be a trap game. This is gonna be a knockout, 60-minute brawl.“

Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Jets in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1900 to win this year’s Super Bowl and 6.5-point favorites in Week 3.

Jets base schemes

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 3 preview: Breaking down the Jets’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Lions attack forward to offset Jets’ aggressiveness

Glenn’s Jets’ defense won’t look like the one he ran in Detroit (the Jets run a 3-4 base with a 2-4 subpackage), but the principles remain the same: Stop the run, press at the line of scrimmage, and take the fight to the offense.

On paper, the Jets defense ranks very highly in most statistics (including allowing the fewest yards per game this season with just 197 total ypg), and on film, they fly to the football in both the run and the pass. They plug rushing lanes up the middle with big space occupiers and downhill linebackers, and also have the range to chase laterally down the line of scrimmage. Against the pass, they play press-man coverage at the line, look comfortable in man and zone schemes, and spread out their coverages to the sidelines with their defensive backs.

The Jets’ aggressiveness has been a key catalyst in their defensive success in 2026, but this approach also leaves them vulnerable in certain areas.

For example, against the run, the Jets ask their defensive tackles to occupy multiple offensive linemen, thus freeing up gap lanes for their linebackers to fill and stop the ball carrier quickly. To offset this, the Lions will need their interior offensive linemen to win one-on-one or run movement-based blocking schemes, such as Duo or pulling guards.

Jared Goff will also need to make quick decisions because the Jets defensive line has the fastest “get off” at the snap (0.71 seconds). That being said, their time to pressure is 2.69 seconds (21st in the NFL), meaning that while the Jets have elite quickness, they can get stuck on blocks, creating opportunities for a decisive quarterback.

Over two weeks, the Jets’ aggressiveness showed up most when the Titans and/or Packers tried to move laterally with quick screens, passes to the flat, or stretch outside zone runs. The Jets are far too quick and athletic, and New York often chewed up these plays. However, with linebackers attacking downhill, the secondary living in two-high safety shells, and the corners pressing the line, there is often space to operate in the middle of the field.

Look for the Lions to be creative with a run-blocking scheme that opens lanes for Gibbs to speed through, and a forward-moving passing approach that attacks the middle of the field with their best skill players, like Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta.

Prediction 2: Lots of 11 personnel, keep Jets defense in nickel

While Glenn ran a ton of “Base” defense in Detroit and a fair amount during his first year with the Jets, their 2026 approach has seen them play more nickel sets (roughly 77% of the time). While this brings them closer to the league average, their production in Base has been higher.

When in a Base defensive set, the Jets have produced impressive numbers, including a -0.58 EPA, best in the NFL. However, when the Jets move to a subpackage look, their production dips, producing a 0.18 EPA and ranking 13th in the NFL. This shows up against both the run and the pass, as they drop from the top of the rankings in Base to the middle of the pack in subpackages.

By running a lot of 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR sets), the Lions will not only get their best skill players on the field at the same time, but it will also help lighten the box, set up cleaner rush lanes, and open up opportunities with play-action and in the intermediate passing game.

Prediction 3: Lions deploy Base defense to stop the run

On the flip side, the Lions will want to stay in their Base defense, especially early in the game, and work to take the Jets’ rushing attack away.

NFL teams strive for a balanced run/pass split with their offensive play calls, but the reality is, this is a passing league, and more often than not, teams default to throwing the ball to gain positive yards quickly. Glenn, like Campbell, wants to control the game with the run, and through two weeks, their run/pass split is roughly 44%/56%, resulting in the eighth-highest rushing rate and fourth-most rushing attempts entering Week 3.

Despite the dedication to and opportunities in the run game, the Jets are only producing 3.3 yards per rushing attempt (28th) with a -0.20 EPA (28th). One main reason for this lack of production is that their offensive line isn’t getting much push. Most blocking calls are one-on-one matchups where the offensive line is asked to win, or simple inside/outside zone calls, and over two games, New York hasn’t shown much creativity in blocking assignments. As a result, about 30% of their runs gain no positive yardage, and their rushing yards before contact are just 0.76 (24th) as a team, and 0.6 for starting running back Breece Hall.

The Jets have shown a dedication to the run, the Lions a dedication to stopping it, and Base defense allows the Lions to get their best run defenders on the field to win this battle in the trenches.

Prediction 4: Lions pass rush turns pressures into sacks

While the Jets’ run blocking has lacked impact, their pass blocking has been very good, as Jeremy Reisman pointed out in his game observations post; the Jets offensive line currently has PFF’s highest pass-blocking grade (77.4).

In Week 1, the Jets didn’t allow a sack to the Titans, and while they did give up four sacks to the Packers, many were coverage-based rather than pressure getting home, as shown by their time-to-pressure allowed numbers (2.76 seconds, 13th in the NFL).

However, the Jets have surrendered 33 pressures through two games (28th), indicating a few things. First, quarterback Geno Smith is holding onto the ball (he averages 2.97 seconds per throw, 7th longest), and his line is holding up just long enough to keep him upright. Second, Smith still has enough mobility (at 35 years old) to stretch his time in the pocket. And lastly, neither the Titans nor the Packers could consistently generate a pass rush that could finish.

Bottom line, the Jets’ offensive line and veteran quarterback have felt some heat, but have mitigated that pressure for the most part.

If the Lions want to disrupt the Jets’ success, they’ll need to turn those pressures into sacks. For this to happen, the Lions will need to keep their aggressive approach on the defensive line, deploying stunts and pulls and continuing to generate pressure at a high rate. Through two games, the Lions’ time to pressure is 2.51 seconds (sixth fastest in the NFL), resulting in 39 pressures (fifth most in the NFL) and seven sacks (fourth).

Entering Week 3, Aidan Hutchinson ranks third in the NFL in pressures (14) and sacks (3), but he’ll need help from his other starting defensive linemen: DJ Wonnum (six pressures, no sacks), Alim McNeill (four pressures, one sack), and Tyleik Williams (four pressures, no sacks).

item.title: Carolina Panthers 2026 fan mailbag: Bryce Young & Brad Idzik evolution, Bobby Okereke surprise, and more!
item.description: Answering all your questions in this week’s fan mailbag!
item.content:encoded:
Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We got the Browns on deck on Sunday coming off a fantastic and complete win last week. The rose colored glasses are on, and hopefully don’t drop off any time soon. So I’m going to answer all of your questions from the week, let’s dive right in!

Forager: Continuing with the optimism and believing the Panthers have their franchise quarterback (I’ll let you pick if it’s Bryce or Haynes :-)), and that they will be picking 32nd in next year’s draft, what position or positions would be on the table for that pick?

Seeing the success Waller is having, maybe a pass-catching TE? Possibly an OG for salary cap concerns? Another edge rusher because injuries seem to love this position?

Its hard to say at this point, but the Panthers definitely seem to prioritize the trenches on both sides of the ball. Depending on where they pick, a center or a guard would make a lot of sense. I can’t imagine they’ll hang on to both Robert Hunt and Damien Lewis as their cap hits get larger. They could again aim for another tackle since Taylor Moton, Ikem Ekwonu, and Rasheed Walker could all be out the door next off-season depending on circumstance.

EDGE rusher is always a thought since this defense tends to rotate them in quite often. I could even see an interior linebacker as a longer term answer to pair with Devin Lloyd. Bobby Okereke has been playing well, but I think he’s more of a stop gap option for the team.

Brice Guild: Brian, I know all the talk is about the play of Lloyd and he has been fun to watch but my biggest surprise has been Okereke. He seems faster and more versatile then I expected. He seems to already, in this new to him defense, playing quick and effective.

Is it just a good scheme match that is allowing him to play faster then last year? What is your expectations for the development of the chemistry between Lloyd and him and their ceiling together as a interior LB pairing.

I think Okereke is definitely a good scheme fit for what Carolina wants out of their interior linebackers, guys who can aggressively pursue the rush and maintain integrity in zone coverage schemes in the pass. I think they’ve developed relatively good chemistry but we’ve also seen both sides of the extremes as far as offenses they’ve faced are concerned. The Bears blew up this defense and the Falcons could barely move the ball without hurting themselves. Let’s see what it looks like in 4-5 weeks for a better answer.

TXPanther: The Panthers hiring Darrell Bevell as associate HC/offensive specialist flew under the radar for most of us… could he be the answer to why the offense looks to have taken a step?

I absolutely think it helped quite a bit. Between hiring the guy that Dave Canales and Brad Idzik cut their teeth under in Seattle, and Dave Canales handing the reigns off to Idzik with Bevell there to support him, I could totally see Bevell being a bigger reason than people realize in this offense being so effective all of a sudden. Both Canales and Idzik call plays that are likely largely based on what they learned during their time serving underneath him.

WanderingJanusz: Is Nic Scourton the Kelvin Benjamin of 2026?

I’m not ready to award this team with the energy of the 2015 Panthers just two weeks into the season. They are 1-1, so they’d have to win every game left in the regular season to match that energy. That said, it is interesting how Ejiro Evero is deploying his defense now that the pass rush isn’t going to passively generate pressure like they would have (in theory) with a fully healthy Scourton in the rotation. He blitzed a lot last week.

@WTMealey: Amongst their peers who would rank higher

BY vs QBs

Canales vs HCs

DM vs GMs

Idzik vs OCs

Meaning if Bryce is top 15 QB but DM is top 5 GM he ranks higher

I would say Dan Morgan vs General Managers, basically because he has two whole offseasons under his belt where many pundits said it was some of the best drafting and maneuvering in free agency they had seen. Right now, Canales, Bryce Young, and Idzik are all kind of starting on new footing. So I’m going with Dan Morgan.

Gunnercrf: How about that lead block by Moehrig on that pick six?! That was so hype he pancaked the guy so bad at the endzone he woke up in a Denny’s. Love seeing defensive players lead blocking for their teammates.

While Tre’Von Moehrig isn’t a traditional safety by any means, he absolutely brings the physicality on just about every play he can. I very much enjoy watching him play. Kind of reminds me of Chris Harris with how he hits at times.

SmoothC: How different would the ATL game be if they had a QB above the level of a moldy pumpkin? The defense still allowed 160 yards rushing.

Taking your starters out in the 4th quarter during a blowout win doesn’t help the rushing numbers in a vacuum. They very much held the Falcons and especially Bijan Robinson in check when it mattered.

SnarkyComet: Brian, curious on your take of a segment on Rich Eisen’s Overreaction Monday (On a Tuesday) this week where it was proposed that Bryce could wind up in the top 5 passers in the NFL this season. Eisen quickly said it wasn’t an overreaction and that he’s been playing great, but he wants to see how Bryce will do against this Browns defense.

Crazy talk or is there something there?

Based on two games worth of information to digest, no it isn’t crazy. Is it objectively an overreaction? Yes, I would say so. Carolina has a lot of good teams on their schedule this season and much better defenses ahead. Combine that with the general wear and tear of the long NFL season likely causing some important starters to miss at least some time, and teams getting more film on Brad Idzik’s tendencies as a play caller, and things could absolutely slow down. But Bryce has built a case so far that he could and should be in that conversation.

JakeNCVA: At least twice this summer (once by me), you were asked if we expected the playcalling to be much different under Idzik than it was under Canales. And if I remember correctly the short answer was no, not really. We have seen the offense be better so far than it was most of the time last season. Well to be more precise, we have seen the passing game be better. Some people are attributing this to Idzik calling for more passes down the field. But that would mean that last season Canales called pass plays that were designed dump offs at the LOS at least half of the time while still sending receivers downfield. Through two games the Panthers offense is averaging almost 40 drop backs at game to around 20 running plays. Yes there have been increased targets to the tight ends in both games – something I imagine Canales and Idzik planned on doing in the offseason. As some of your CSR counterparts have said — it appears the game has slowed down for Bryce. Canales said “Bryce has taken advantage of the looks he has gotten”. Is it really the play calling or more like both Bryce Young and the receivers have both improved this season.

I’ll be happy to get my receipts for not being correct necessarily in my prediction. However, I do think its a combination of Brad Idzik encouraging more aggression and Bryce Young simply being way more comfortable and confident. They were running similar down field concepts in 2025, and sometimes Bryce just didn’t throw them and elected to play it safe. But by the same token, I don’t know how much Canales was gearing him towards playing it more safe than letting it rip. We certainly saw Bryce let it rip at times in 2025, but he’s been really dealing the ball. I almost feel like we’re seeing an evolution of Canales’s game plans with some higher urgency to score now rather than simply keep the Panthers in the game.

That’s all for this week Panthers fans. Enjoy the Browns game, and KEEP POUNDING!

item.title: Ed Policy may regret not waiting on Matt LaFleur, Brian Gutenkunst contracts
item.description: After Ed Policy succeeded Mark Murphy as the president and CEO of the Packers, it quickly became clear that 2025 would be an up-or-out season for coach Matt LaFleur and G.M.
item.content:encoded:
After Ed Policy succeeded Mark Murphy as the president and CEO of the Packers, it quickly became clear that 2025 would be an up-or-out season for coach Matt LaFleur and G.M. Brian Gutekunst.

Both had contracts running through 2026. Policy made it clear that he's not a fan of lame-duck arrangements. So either they'd be extended or fired after the 2025 season.

Ultimately, the Packers made it to the playoffs as the No. 7 seed in the NFC, before blowing a 21-3 halftime lead against the Bears in the wild-card round.

That was enough, after a brief period of uncertainty, to get the Packers the give LaFleur and Gutekunst new contracts. Which, assuming that the deals guarantee one or more full seasons beyond 2026, complicates any consideration of firing either or both of them this year.

So what was the rush to extend them? There was a time when having a lame-duck coach undermined him, because the players may not respond in the desired way to a coach who may be gone after the season ends. And it's possible that Ed Policy clings to that notion in part because his father, Carmen, firmly believed in that approach when he was running the 49ers and the Browns.

Nowadays, there's a different reality in NFL locker rooms. Pro football has become a year-to-year reality, with continuity not guaranteed. The coach may be gone next year, and plenty of the players may be gone next year. All that matters is this year.

For the Packers, their coach and G.M. have a layer of job security they wouldn't have enjoyed without the extensions. It takes off some of the pressure to perform at the highest possible level, especially because firing them — and buying out their contracts — becomes a challenge for a publicly-owned team that has been, through Policy, complaining about the financial realities of a league in which the other franchises can carve off slivers of equity for many millions in new revenue.

That doesn't mean LaFleur and Gutekunst are safe. But, if they get fired, they'll get their buyouts. And the Packers will have to pay them while also paying their replacements.

In hindsight, the right move would have been to press pause on the extensions. It's a lesson both for Policy and for other owners who may end up on the fence as to the question of whether a contract should be extended in order to avoid having the coach or the G.M. work through the last year of their deals.

When in doubt, the best move may be to wait it out.

item.title: To kick or receive? NFL coaches still haven't figured out the overtime coin toss
item.description: The NFL changed overtime to guarantee both teams a possession, but that created a new strategic puzzle.
item.content:encoded:
Prior to overtime last Sunday night, with his team in jeopardy of starting a pivotal season with two straight losses, Indianapolis Colts coach Shane Steichen contemplated one of the toughest choices in football. 

He had to decide whether to kick or receive if the Colts won the coin toss. 

Winning the overtime coin toss used to be cause for celebration under the NFL's previous rules. The receiving team gained the opportunity to secure victory without its opponent touching the ball if it scored a touchdown on its opening possession. 

The optimal strategy is far murkier now that the NFL's overtime system guarantees both teams possession of the ball. Winning the coin toss now means choosing between taking the ball first to chase a potential possession advantage or playing defense first to know exactly how many points are required to win. 

The presence of quarterback Patrick Mahomes in the opposing huddle influenced Steichen's decision to give the Kansas City Chiefs the ball to start Sunday's overtime. As Steichen told reporters after the game, "If we go first with it, Mahomes gets four downs going the other way, so we wanted to play defense there and know we had four downs." 

Steichen's decision backfired on the Colts when both teams settled for field goals on their initial possessions of overtime and Mahomes took advantage of getting the ball a second time. Harrison Butker's game-clinching 40-yard field goal sent the Chiefs spilling onto the field in celebration and sparked renewed debate over how teams should approach winning the overtime coin toss. 

It's difficult to draw meaningful conclusions from the results of recent overtime games because the sample size is too small. Twenty games have gone to overtime since the NFL adopted the new rules for the playoffs in March 2022 and then extended them to the regular season in 2025. The team that won the overtime coin toss has chosen to kick in 14 of those 20 games. And yet the team that received the ball first is 11-8-1 (57.5%).  

A study published by a football-obsessed cardiologist in The Journal of Sports Analytics this past July offered some of the first mathematical insight into the optimal strategy for the NFL's kick-or-receive overtime coin toss dilemma. Using a Monte Carlo simulation to predict which strategy would prove advantageous over 100,000 NFL overtimes, author Dylan Goings found that electing to receive the ball first would produce a win rate of 53.14%.

"Coaches who choose to kick are trading a structural positioning advantage for informational clarity that, in our analysis, does not translate to improved outcomes," Goings concluded.

Goings told Yahoo Sports he took on the project in his spare time last January after he and some college buddies got into a spirited debate over whether the Chicago Bears were right to kick the ball to the Rams at the start of overtime in the divisional playoffs. The cardiologist could not let the argument go unresolved, especially not when his background in medical research, risk stratification and statistical analysis gave him the tools to find a definitive answer.

"It's just the type of person I am," Goings said with a laugh. "If you have an argument with a friend and you have a hunch that you're right, let's settle it.

"I had already written code to do a Monte Carlo analysis for something very similar. So with just a few tweaks I had something that's relevant to football fans."

The key limitation to a Monte Carlo simulation — an analysis that uses random guessing over and over to predict the possible outcomes of an event — is that the results are only as good as the assumptions and probabilities that the researcher feeds into the simulation. Goings combatted that before submitting his study for publication by posting the results of his Monte Carlo simulation to a handful of Reddit forums and incorporating feedback on how heavily to weigh variables like two-point conversion strategy or clock pressure. 

"It was like a peer review process from strangers on the internet," Goings said.

To test whether the optimal strategy varied if one team had an elite defense or a turnover-prone quarterback or a shaky kicker, Goings conducted a sensitivity analysis using extreme or even unrealistic efficiencies. There was no combination of variables, he said, where he found it was more advantageous to kick than to receive. 

The best way for the team that has the ball second in overtime to eat into its disadvantage, according to Goings, is to aggressively go for the win on its initial possession. Whether by going for it on 4th-and-short instead of kicking a tying field goal or attempting a two-point conversion instead of kicking a tying extra point, those options are superior to matching scores and giving the opposing team possession of the ball in the sudden death format.

One of the most qualified people to assess Goings' findings might be a former backgammon world champion with a passion for game theory. Frank Frigo has worked with risk-averse NFL and college coaches to help them optimize their in-game decision making, first as a co-founder of data analysis firm EdjSports and now as an independent consultant.

When asked which strategy he favored for the overtime coin toss winner, Frigo told Yahoo Sports that he believes the potential to have a greater number of possessions by taking the ball first slightly outweighed the informational advantage of getting the ball second. Frigo hasn't run a full data simulation like Goings, but he pointed to data showing that 22.1% of NFL overtimes end on the third possession and 6.4% on the fifth.

"It's hard for me to imagine that the informational advantage of having the ball second outweighs that," Frigo said.

As fans in Buffalo know all too well, the NFL implemented its new overtime system in response to the Kansas City Chiefs beating the star-crossed Bills in the divisional round of the NFL playoffs in January 2022. After a thrilling, back-and-forth 60 minutes of regulation, the overtime coin flip had an outsize influence on the outcome. The Chiefs won the toss, and Mahomes promptly led them to a touchdown on the opening drive of overtime, stranding Josh Allen on the sideline with no way to respond, no way to impact the result. 

The lack of debate over whether the kicking or receiving team has the advantage in overtime now is proof that the NFL's new system is working. Since the start of the 2025 regular season, the overtime coin toss winner has a record of 6-12-1.To this day, teams don't seem to fully understand how to capitalize on the slight structural advantage of receiving the ball first or how to negate much of the disadvantage of taking the ball second by playing for the win.

After his team lost 20-17 in overtime to the Green Bay Packers last Sunday, New York Jets coach Aaron Glenn struggled to explain to reporters why he elected to receive the ball first in overtime. Glenn said the Jets were hoping to eat most of the 10-minute clock with their opening drive, score a touchdown and put pressure on the Packers to answer. 

"It didn't happen for us the way that I planned," Glenn conceded.

Aaron Glenn says he wanted to control the clock in deciding to take the ball first in overtime:

"It didn't happen for us the way that I planned." pic.twitter.com/2grHad0Q77

— SNY Jets (@snyjets) September 20, 2026

Later that night, Steichen also faced a barrage of questions about why he chose to kick a game-tying field goal at the end of the Colts' lone overtime possession rather than going for it on 4th-and-8 deep in Kansas City territory. Steichen initially sent his offense onto the field, only to gesture to quarterback Daniel Jones not to snap the ball.

"Had a play called, [but] had to love the look to run it there," Steichen said. "And, if not, obviously we took the delay of game there and kicked the field goal to tie it."

#Colts head coach Shane Steichen on the decision to kick a field goal instead of going for it on 4th & 8 in overtime, tying the score at 30-30.

The Chiefs would go on to kick a game-winning field goal on the following drive. pic.twitter.com/inbqYFaqMH

— WISH-TV News (@WISHNews8) September 21, 2026

To Goings, the most egregious overtime coin flip decision this season was his favorite team's. Having either not read Goings' study or not agreed with his conclusions, New Orleans Saints coach Kellen Moore — after winning the toss — chose to kick the ball to Detroit in a 31-30 week 1 overtime loss to the Lions. 

"They did the exact opposite of the strategy I suggested," Goings lamented. "That was pretty frustrating to watch."

item.title: Andrew Janocko is excited for the return of Brock Bowers

The Las Vegas Raiders are off to a 2-0 start without their superstar tight end, Brock Bowers. Klint Kubiak has kept the offense afloat, averaging 26 points per game while the former Georgia Bulldog has missed time.

“Yeah, he’s a tremendous player, brings a unique set of skills,
both in the run and pass game. Something that as he as he progresses and gets ready to go again, we’re
excited when he’s ready to go to get him back.“

Janocko sees the confidence growing during Bowers’ absence the first two weeks. He thinks it has made offense better as a unit.

“I think it gives everybody confidence that everybody can go in, do their job in the way
we see fit. That they can go in, they can play different guys, can play different positions. We can maximize
different skill sets in different ways and execute the offense.”

With Bowers back, the Raiders have a chance to start 3-0 for the first time since 2021. That 3-0 team went on to play in the NFL Wildcard round. Bowers on the field makes it all possible.

item.title: 5 things to watch as Jets face Lions in Week 3 of 2026 NFL season
item.description: Here are the main storylines to watch as the New York Jets look bounce back against the Detroit Lions in Week 3
item.content:encoded:
The Jets suffered a setback in Week 2 as they blew a 10-point fourth quarter lead against the Green Bay Packers.

They have a chance to bounce back against another NFC North team this weekend as they travel to Detroit to face the 1-1 Detroit Lions.

Here are the storylines to watch as the Jets look to improve to 2-1…

Aaron Glenn vs. Dan Campbell

Glenn was the defensive coordinator for the first four years of Dan Campbell's tenure as the Lions' head coach.

This weekend, they face off against each other with the winner set to improve to 2-1.

Both men have mutual respect for one another and will ensure that their team knows exactly what to expect. It may be difficult for either coach to spring any surprises on their former colleague, so this game could come down to who executes best.
