It goes down as an explosive play as it is a run play once Caleb decides to tuck it and go. This was his second of three explosive runs on the day and the first off a scramble. A good decision to go after working through his progression and he knew where the sticks were to keep this drive going early in the third by taking contact and pushing through for the first. It’s the second explosive run of the series.

Explosive Play 2.4 – Q3 13:28, 1st and 10 from the Minnesota 42. Kyle Monangai off right end for 15 yard gain.

The third explosive run of the drive and the first for Monangai. This is one of those runs where you look back and think…why did he not have 30 carries in this one? The Bears use 12 personnel here, with both Loveland and Kmet on the right hand side of the line with Odunze split out wide. Monangai runs through contact trying to poke out the ball around the line of scrimmage and bursts through the hole before dragging the corner for about six additional yards and another set of downs.

Explosive Play 2.5 – Q3 12:14, 2nd and 6 from the Minnesota 23. Kyle Monangai off right guard for 12 yards.

The fourth explosive run on the drive and the second for Monangai. Just two plays after the 15 yarder, the Bears use Cole Kmet as a full back and line up in the I-formation. Blocking action moves to the right with Kmet filling the edge defender on the left. Monangai starts the action to the right and makes a cut back to the middle of the field. He’s untouched for ten yards before falling forward for a couple extra. Well blocked here by the Bears. Unbelievably, the four explosive runs on the same drive would not lead to points as D’Andre Swift would fumble at the one a few plays later.

Explosive Play 2.6 – Q3 5:19, 3rd and 6 from the Chicago 17. Caleb Williams scrambles off left end for 10 yards.

It’s not worth spending a ton of time breaking down scrambles but again I think this is an aspect of Caleb’s game that we can appreciate him flexing when needed. The concern with the hamstring injury going forward is if he’ll feel comfortable running and if so, will he be able to shift into high gear.

Anyway, love the spin move here and my mind automatically added a Chris Berman sound effect when he did it.

Explosive Play 2.7 – Q4 11:43, 3rd and 7 from the Chicago 36. Caleb Williams passes short left to D’Andre Swift for 32 yards.

A well-timed screen on 3rd down here. It’s a nice play design with a WR screen set up on the right side, where Caleb gives a pump fake, before coming back to Swift on the left side. Swift has a couple of blockers who don’t really impact the play here. He is able to make the first defender miss at the sticks before breaking away from a second defender who goes for the strip. He’s not quite able to run away from the third defender before being taken down for a monster gain. The play design earned the first but Swift again took it from a nice play to an explosive.

Explosive Play 2.8 – Q4 0:38, 2nd and 10 from the Minnesota 41. Tyson Bagent completes pass deep right to Rome Odunze for 21 yards.

This is a nice route from Rome in the waning seconds of the game. Bagent is a little late getting this one out and the velocity of the pass allows the defender to recover. Rome does a nice job bringing in the football against his body, fighting through the contact, and getting out of bounds to stop the clock. We know that Bagent’s arm strength isn’t going to be able to deliver a ball at pace in this situation so he’ll need to deliver that one in the future a touch quicker. Nice play overall from Rome knowing the situation and fighting to move forward to stop the clock. A running clock there would’ve shorted the Bears multiple shots to the end zone.

2026 Explosive Play Count: D’Andre Swift 4, Kyle Monangai 4, Caleb Williams 4, Rome Odunze 2, and one each for Kalif Raymond, Luther Burden, and Cole Kmet.

What was your favorite explosive play from the opener? There’s something beautiful about Kyle Monangai dragging defenders – he’s got my vote for the week.

item.title: Dolphins’ Chop Robinson to start wearing Guardian Cap after latest concussion
item.description: After five documented concussions, Robinson to begin wearing extra protection.
item.content:encoded:
Miami Dolphins third-year pass rusher Chop Robinson missed last Sunday’s loss to the San Francisco 49ers due to a concussion he suffered during practice leading up to the game. According to Robinson, it was his fifth documented concussion — third as a member of the Dolphins.

On Thursday, speaking with the South Florida media, Robinson said that as a result of his latest brain injury, he will begin wearing a padded Guardian Cap moving forward in an effort to prevent further concussions.

“Just for me personally, I’m starting with a Guardian Cap, so I’m being smart about it,” said Robinson. “I want a future and [to] have kids and have a family and everything. So, I’ll just put the Guardian Cap [on]. There’s no harm in wearing it, so I might as well put it on.”

When speaking on the incident that caused his concussion during practice, Robinson said that it was “just a football hit,” but declined to further elaborate.

According to an independent study, Guardian Caps can reduce incidences of concussions by 54-62%.

We will continue to keep you updated on all things Miami Dolphins as the team prepares to battle the Kansas City Chiefs at Hard Rock Stadium this Sunday.

item.title: Tucker Kraft on Packers fans booing: 'It's not gonna help us win'
item.description: The Packers were booed off Lambeau Field during their Thursday night loss to the Falcons.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers dropped to 1-2 on the season after a 35-14 defeat to the Atlanta Falcons on "Thursday Night Football." It wasn't the best home opener and the crowd at Lambeau Field let the players know by serenading them with boos during the game.

Many of the Packers players understood the frustration from the fans and understood they as a team did not do anything to change the mood inside the stadium.

Tight end Tucker Kraft, who caught four passes for 26 yards, said hearing the boos was "pretty disappointing" and didn't understand the crowd turning on the home side.

"That's pretty tough," Kraft said via ESPN's Matt Schneidman. "Everyone pictures Lambeau Field and not boos. I don't picture boos when I picture my home stadium. That's tough. It's pretty disappointing. Especially for a home opener. It's pretty disappointing. It's not gonna help us win. I don't know what people think, that's gonna rally us or something like that. But we're grown men. We're mentally strong enough, capable enough to get back on the field and play ball. But it'd probably be much easier with the 70,000 people behind us rather than opposing us."

OOF! THE REACTIONS FROM THE PACKER FAN BASE RIGHT NOW.

NOT LOOKING GOOD, SHOWERS OF BOOs pic.twitter.com/O8vPMxV1mW

— ClutchWire (@ClutchWireHQ) September 25, 2026

The lone victory through three games is the worst start the Packers have had under head coach Matt LaFleur in eight seasons. The offensive line is banged up. The running game, which totaled 17 yards against the Falcons, was nonexistent. And the Packers had the ball for 15 fewer minutes in the game than the Falcons.

LaFleur, whose seat is heating up, was at a loss afterward, saying, "I don't know what we're doing well offensively."

Kraft added they're only three games into the season and there's a lot of football left to be played.

"We can't let external noise divide us," Kraft said. "Us guys in this locker room, we're really all we've got. We spend a lot of time together, so just continue to stay close and build off each other."

The Packers will return to action in Week 4 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers before welcoming the Chicago Bears and the Dallas Cowboys to Lambeau Field.

item.title: #PostPulpit mailbag: What problems will the Jaguars present Drake Maye?
item.description: The latest edition of our Patriots mailbag answers questions about the Jaguars defense, recent injuries, and more.
item.content:encoded:
After a Week 2 victory that came with the injury bug, the New England Patriots are set to head down to Jacksonville for a Week 3 matchup with the Jaguars.

So, let’s get into this week’s #PostPulpit Mailbag.

What defensive schemes do the Jags run? How are the coverage corners? Will we see some man? How good are they in 2 deep zone? Have they effectively run cover 6? What’s their blitz rate? How effective are they at just rushing 4? What did the Broncos do to turn that game around and put up 17 unanswered? How are the Jags vs stopping the run? – Maye The Force Be With You

Jaguars defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile has quite the coaching background, having come up under defensive coaches Vic Fangio, Brian Flores, Jeff Hafley and other respected defensive minds.

“He’s got his own style. I’ll say that,” offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels said. “I know where he’s come from and who he’s been subjected to and I’m sure he’s learned an immense amount from those people. But he’s got his own personality. You can see it on the film. There’s games where they do some different things and challenge you schematically.”

Similar to Fangio, Campanile leans heavily on zone coverages, running them more than 75% of the time. And speaking of the infamous Cover 6, the Jaguars have used it at the second-highest rate (19.6%) in the NFL since 2025 — only behind Fangio himself — with strong results. Campanile’s background under Flores then shows up in his exotic blitz packages, where Jacksonville sends extra rushers at the ninth-highest rate in the NFL (36.7%).

As for their personnel, Jacksonville has a unique rotation in its secondary, with four cornerbacks — Montaric Brown, Jarring Jones, Travis Hunter and Jourdan Lewis — each playing between 53% and 77% of the defensive snaps. Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker bookend the defensive front — a good, but not great unit like the Patriots have played the first two weeks.

The scheme and aggressiveness have led to plenty of turnovers, with Jacksonville forcing three in two games after ranking second in the NFL last season with 31. But that aggression can also be exploited, as the Jaguars have been one of the NFL’s worst deep-pass defenses through two games. Denver also found success getting Bo Nix on the move, something the Patriots could look to replicate with Drake Maye.

I have a feeling the injury to Onwenu could prove to be a disaster for the Offensive Line. I thought Van Roten was scary awful when Onwenu went down. Will they give someone else a shot next week. Like Walter Rouse, they even had Lomu play some Guard in camp. Will Lomu, Rouse, or someone else get a chance at Guard? – Elderly Lothario

It certainly wasn’t perfect in relief on Sunday for Van Roten, who admitted he was a bit rusty, but we’ll give him some grace getting thrown into the fire just weeks after signing with the team. The veteran played solid football at right guard for the Giants last season and I’d expect him to continue to get the opportunity to hold that spot in Onwenu’s absence. His experience playing next to Morgan Moses should also help.

As for Lomu, I would prioritize continuing to get him ready at tackle. It could be an option down the line, something Mike Vrabel did not rule out, as well as a few other options.

“So, we will get [Van Roten] working there with Morgan [Moses]. I think Walter [Rouse] will get some opportunities to go there and practice,” Vrabel said. “Walter Rouse is a player we got from Minnesota who has been working really hard, and we will see how he does. Ben Brown is back and working. So, we’ll get a bunch of guys in there the next couple days and try to make a decision.”

The Pats offensive line has been a headline for years. Almost always a concern. Is it the same for the other NFL teams but we don’t hear about it or is there more stability on other teams? – funnyattimes

Outside of a few teams around the league who have found consistency up front, this is life in the NFL up front. There simply aren’t enough good offensive lineman, specifically tackles, in football today and the lack of padded practices over the offseason make it harder to develop the position.

With Woodson and Pettus injured what are the chances we try to sign John Saunders Jr. off of the Jets Practice Squad? – naplesme

Pettus landed on injured reserve with a high-ankle sprain. As for Woodson, he was spotted in the locker room this week without a sling — which he wore post game — and avoided injured reserve. Still, he did not practice Wednesday and Thursday and seems set to miss this Sunday.

As for Saunders, I would have kept him around on the practice squad in the first place after an impressive summer. The fact they did not and signed other safeties in the process would indicate to me they will role with Mike Brown off of the practice squad.

Any chance of adding to our tight end depth via a trade or is it too soon for that path? – jpd985

Eli Raridon’s (thigh) status is worth watching this week after he was downgraded from a limited participant on Wednesday to a did not participate on Thursday. If he can’t go, Cameron Latu and Tanner Arkin remain on the 53-man roster.

With Raridon’s injury not a long-term issue, that group appears to be fine to move forward with. They did also add tight end Tanner Conner to the practice squad this week.

I know it’s hard to say, but realistically how guys on IR with designation do we really think 1) will come back, 2) be able to contribute and 3) before the season is too late? – Patriot in Chicago

Among the nine players on injured reserve, Julian Hill, Jeremiah Webb, and Myles Montgomery will miss the entire season being placed on IR during the offseason. As for the rest of the group, I’d expect them all back at some point except for Mike Onwenu (outside of a potential return during a deep playoff).

That means A.J. Brown, Marcus Bryant, Khalil Jacobs, Dell Pettus, and Bryce Baringer will return at some point. Obviously Brown is the big one, but I’d expect the majority, or all, of that group to contribute as depth pieces and on special teams.

How concerned are you about the Pat’s dwindling salary cap? Seems to be around $6 Million left, and that doesn’t leave much room for October trade deadline maneuvers to backfill or upgrade down the stretch. – WannaBe Pats GM

No concern. As always the salary cap can easily be tinkered with and any midseason addition should not come with a large price tag.

A lot of doom and gloom going around due to the series of injuries. What positive regression do we have to look forward to this year? And where is the team improving/has room to improve? – LandenPatz1

I do not believe the Drake Maye we’ve seen through two games is the version of the quarterback we’ll see the rest of the season. He’s too good of a player to continue making the early season mistakes and should settle in with new players around him.

From there, the Patriots defense has certainly been a positive through two weeks. While it has come in matchups vs. Drew Lock and 42-year old Aaron Rodgers, I’d say the encouraging sign is that they’ve seemed to find their blueprint of a man blitz defense. With Christian Gonzalez and the group of corners they have, keep it coming.

That’s all for this week’s #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you’d liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow@iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

item.title: Three Reasons With The Earl: Miami Dolphins Hope, Concern Week 3
item.description: There never was much hope… just a fool’s hope.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 season looks rough for the Miami Dolphins. They were outclassed against an NFC contender and now turn around to face Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs. There is not going to be much hope to be found this season. But dagnabbit, I will squeeze what little hope I can out of this team. Just for you’uns (pronounced ‘yuns’). Like I said last week, I’m going to focus on areas that may not be major talking points elsewhere e.g. Patrick Mahomes.

3 REASONS FOR HOPE

SOMEONE CALL OSHA… BUT NOT FOR ME!


The Dolphins get their first home game of the season and that hot Miami sun will likely be a factor. The projected weather report says mid 80s for the game, and that sun and heat will still be a factor, as it always is. Home cooking is always a positive factor in the NFL. Sure, the Dolphins fans may not be as enthusiastic about the team this year and may not pack the stadium, but home games are still beneficial to the host regardless. Last week, Miami controlled the time of possession by a slight margin overall, but considerably more in the 1st half. They held a 19:17 to 10:43 lead in TOP. They also had scoring opportunities they just didn’t capitalize on. If they can lean on the run game and control the clock in the Miami weather, the Chiefs defense will start to wear down. And in the NFL, all it takes is an opportunity or two for a big play to turn a game around.

THE CHIEFS HIT THE ROAD


The Chiefs are coming off a two primetime contests at home, including an overtime SNF contest against the Colts. Arrowhead is a notoriously dominant home field advantage, but now they must travel to the east coast to play a 1PM EST game. The Chiefs are a good team and should be favored – as they are – but road games in the NFL, even against bad teams, are still tough to win. Coach Hafley has started to get tougher on this team and he mentioned that despite the youth and talent deficiencies, they are playing harder, tougher, and with good intensity and teams are noticing that. A young, hungry team wanting to impress their coach and get him his first W of the season at home might make for a punch in the mouth the Chiefs aren’t expecting. Add that in with the weather factor, this could be a tougher out than imagined for the favored team.

AN OPPORTUNITY FOR REDEMPTION


Last week I mentioned that the 49ers did not generate much pressure against the Rams. Though the Rams have a better OL than the Dolphins, I still thought Miami had an opportunity to keep Willis cleaner than they did against the Raiders. Well, they kinda did and kinda didn’t. Willis was pressured often, mostly due to issue with one particular offensive lineman. But 2 of the sacks Willis had were him running out of bounds behind the line of scrimmage. He should have thrown the ball away if we are being honest. We can also say he’s becoming a runner at that point. But it goes on the stat sheet as a sack. The 49ers only got Willis on the ground twice and that’s with a premier pass rusher in Nick Bosa. The 49ers also don’t blitz at a high rate, so when they did, they caught the Dolphins in a bind. The Chiefs do not have a premier edge rusher. They have 3 sacks on the season, with 2 coming from the edge group. George Karlaftis III is the most productive of the group with 30.5 career sacks. Felix Anudike-Uzomah has 4 career sacks with 3 of them prior to 2026. Ashton Gillotte is a second-year player with 1.5 career sacks and R. Mason Thomas is a rookie with 1 sack on the season. The Dolphins have faced the likes of Maxx Crosby and Bosa and now get a less prominent group. That doesn’t mean they are bad and won’t generate pressure, but they haven’t proven to be the weapons the Dolphins have seen so far. They do have Chris Jones as an interior rusher, but that’s not an issue for the OTs. The Chiefs also blitz at a higher rate. They are 5th in the league at 39.4% (Miami faces Brian Flores and the Vikings next week who lead the league in blitz rate at a whopping 81.8%). The Raiders and the Niners blitz in the 22% range. Why is this fact a positive? Because the Dolphins can expect and plan for it. They can build in protections and outlets to get the ball out of Willis’ hands quicker to take advantage of the blitzes. The Chiefs have faced two QBs this season who have decent scrambling ability. But neither have the rushing ability that Willis possesses. A poorly timed blitz could get Willis out on the edge and into the secondary before they know it. It will be up to Slowik and Willis to account for this and use it wisely.

BONUS REASON: Watch this reel: https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdmCOhxkVLE/?stkn=MTlwaXcxcXpidW5tOQ==

REASONS FOR CONCERN

THE CHIEFS HAVE A RUNNING GAME


If I asked you where you think Miami falls defensively in terms of yards allowed, where do think it would be? Dead last right? Ackchyually, they are middle of the pack. They are 19th in yards allowed overall and 18th in both passing and rushing yards allowed. Given how both Vegas and San Fran tap-danced their way up and down the field, I would have thought the Dolphins would be league worst. But you know who is league worst? The Indianapolis Colts, the team the Chiefs just beat on SNF. Part of that is pass defense, but both Chiefs’ opponents this season are bottom 4 in rushing yards allowed and yards per attempt allowed. That’s because they faced off against the league’s leading rusher and reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker. Walker has 290 rushing yards on 47 carries in 2 games. The Chiefs are leaning on him and he’s producing. The Dolphins quietly had a solid day against the rushing attack of the 49ers. They gave up 3 rushing TDs, but both main RBs for SF had 48 yards on 17 carries. It was QB Brock Purdy leading the way with 3 scrambles for 30 yards. This game will look more like week 1 where the Raiders leaned on Ashton Jeanty, who went 23 for 102. In a game where heat and TOP will be a factor, the Chiefs will likewise try to take advantage of it with their new weapon. The Dolphins are near the top of the league in missed tackles with only 9. The Broncos and Colts are the bottom two at 27 and 22 respectively. Some of that may be on the defenders. But Walker is tied for 2nd in the league in broken tackles with 6 and is 1st in yards after contact with 199. He is 2nd in YAC/att at 4.2. Much of the talk will be about Mahomes, but Walker is the imminent threat.

NO CALEB DOUGLAS = NO BUENO


The emergence of Caleb Douglas has been the best story from an offseason and young season that offers little in the way of positives for the Dolphins. The 49ers have a solid pass defense, and they limited Douglas to 2 catches for 19 yards, with the second catch not coming until midway into the 4Q. He’s a rookie and we expect some ups and downs. The problem is after that catch, Douglas went down with an injury, which appeared to be an ankle injury. He limped off and was walking on the sideline, so perhaps it’s not too severe. But he has not practiced yet this week. If he misses the game or is limited, the Dolphins will have little to lean on in the way of the passing game. Malik Washington has had some moments where he got open, but the Chiefs play Cover-1(man) 25.8% of the time, their highest usage of typical coverages. The Dolphins don’t have guys that can beat man coverage on a consistent basis. Douglas is their best chance. Not only that, but the Chiefs have the 4th best passing defense in terms of yards allowed and in yards per attempt allowed. They are 9th in passer rating allowed. They are tied with several teams for 3rd place with only 2 passing TDs allowed. If they stuff the Dolphins run game, the offense may not get off the ground without Douglas. The silver lining is that both TDs the Chiefs’ pass defense allowed were to TEs. Maybe this is the week for Slowik to dial up some plays for Dulcich.

YET ANOTHER PLAY CALLER TO WORRY ABOUT


Last week, the Dolphins had to deal with Kyle Shanahan. This week, the Dolphins get yet another offensive mastermind in Andy Reid. The Dolphins’ defense has so much inexperience and in a way, it’s good they face play callers like Shanahan and Reid so early in their careers. They will learn and use the tape to get better for the future. But it is painful in the moment. Last week, the Niners were 5-7 on 3rd down and didn’t have a failed conversion until the 4Q. Brock Purdy only had 2 incompletions on the day and averaged 13 YPA. Do you think Andy Reid will have some plays and looks the young Dolphins defense isn’t ready for? With a better QB and now a dominant rushing attack?

I SAID WHAT I SAID


Once again, I’m not here to push hopium on you that the Dolphins will somehow pull out a W this week. I mean, any given Sunday, but once again, it’s a case of being outclassed on both sides of the ball, especially with Douglas’ status up in the air. What we should be looking for is improvement on both sides of the ball. Can the defense hold down Kenneth Walker? Can the offense move the ball effectively again? Can they put TDs on the board instead of FGs? If so, maybe this will be a closer contest and show the Dolphins are starting to move in the right direction. Anyway, here is the weekend listen for you’uns.

item.title: Ravens vs Saints Rookie Report
item.description: Checking in on the rookies after their first career NFL loss
item.content:encoded:
The Ravens’ 2026 rookie class suffered their first NFL loss in the home opener against the New Orleans Saints in Week 2. Let’s see how the rookies did in the game.

OG Vega Ioane

After a strong NFL debut in Week 1, Ioane had a much rougher time in Week 2. Ioane was charted with four pressures on 40 pass-blocking snaps according to PFF. The Saints countered the new Ravens under-center offense with a lot of A-gap blitzes and Ioane, paired with center Jovaughn Gywn, struggled to sort through the noise. PFF also gave him a low run-blocking grade, but the Ravens ran the ball effectively on Sunday, with clips showing Ioane moving bodies, so I’m not buying into that grade as much. While many, myself included, touted Ioane as one of the most NFL-ready prospects in the draft with an All-Pro ceiling, he’s still just a rookie in his second start next to a first-time starter at center. I’m not discouraged. His Week 1 performance was great, and I’ll buy we see more games like that than this one.

DE Zion Young

Young had an up-and-down day against New Orleans. He continued to flash that raw strength that is the cornerstone of his game, which gave him one pressure on seven pass-rush snaps according to PFF rate, with a 16.3% win rate. He graded out fairly well in pass rush (63.1), run defense (68.7), and special teams (72.6). That being said, Young had two noticeable mistakes on Sunday. First, on the Saints’ first scoring drive, Tyler Shough absolutely shook Young out of his cleats on what should have been an easy tackle for loss that could have helped force a longer field goal attempt. Then, after the Ravens responded to that field goal with their own touchdown and should have been going into halftime with a 14-3 lead, Young failed to keep contain with Malaki Starks on the kick return right before halftime, which allowed the Saints to tag on another three. These aren’t massive mistakes and most rookies do make them, but they were impactful and it’s the little details that can win or lose you a game. Otherwise, I think Young has been as advertised — a guy who’s been able to knock linemen back with his incredible play strength and push the pocket.

WR Elijah Sarratt

After being specifically mentioned by the coaching staff before the game against New Orleans as a guy who could find rhythm with Zay Flowers and Ja’Kobi Lane down, Sarratt got the game-day activation after being a healthy scratch Week 1. Sarratt then proceeded to get zero snaps on offense or special teams. This is frustrating, considering the Ravens did lose and how much they’ve struggled on offense since Flowers went down. Sarratt’s steady hands should be utilized.

TE Matt Hibner and TE Josh Cuevas

I wouldn’t normally put two rookies together, but that’s how little they were both used in this one. Neither tight end saw a target, and they played a combined 24 snaps total against the Saints. Hibner ran 10 routes according to TruMedia and earned a 57.8 run-blocking grade on nine blocking snaps, per PFF. Cuevas ran four routes and had a run-blocking grade of 59.7 on one snap. I specifically mentioned Hibner a couple of times leading up to the game, as I would have liked to have seen him get targets. Fellow tight end Mark Andrews was effective in his safety valve role but didn’t offer much downfield or after the catch. Hibner seems to be a guy who could become an explosive tight end receiving option for this team but hasn’t received much a chance. We’ll have to see if his role gets bigger as the Ravens continue to navigate operating without Flowers and Lane.

CB Chandler Rivers

After being a healthy scratch Week 1, Rivers got the activation against the Saints following T.J. Tampa’s move to IR. Rivers immediately factored into the rotation, out-snapping both Chido Awuzie and Keyon Martin. Rivers flashed throughout the day in coverage, limiting yards after the catch and being a solid tackler — something the rest of the Ravens’ defense struggled with against the Saints. Coming out of the draft, some of the best things scouted from Rivers were his physicality despite his smaller stature, play recognition and IQ, and how well he got downhill to bust screens and on blitzes. That was exactly what he showed in this game, especially on his tackle for loss in the red zone, where he immediately eliminated an Alvin Kamara designed touch out near the boundary. Expect Rivers to keep his playing time in a secondary that’s still looking to find its footing.

P Ryan Eckley

After a great Week 1 where all three of his punts pinned the Colts inside the 20, Eckley’s day against the Saints was less banner-worthy. Eckley only averaged 41.3 yards on his three punts, and none were even caught inside of the 20. With Flowers’ absence continuing to linger, this Ravens team might need to lean on its defense for some wins. That starts with Eckley giving opposing teams a long field to drive on. He’ll need to be better moving forward.

Wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane and running back Adam Randall remain on injured reserve, with defensive tackle Rayshaun Benny on the practice squad.

item.title: Domecoming 20 Years Later: The Night the Saints and New Orleans Came Home
item.description: Twenty years after their emotional return to the Superdome, the Saints’ enduring bond with New Orleans remains as strong as ever.
item.content:encoded:
On Nov. 1, 1966, the National Football League awarded the city of New Orleans a professional football franchise. At exactly 11:11 a.m., then-NFL commissioner Pete Rozelle delivered the words that would forever change the city: “Professional football has voted a franchise to the state of Louisiana, the city of New Orleans.”

The team would later be named the Saints, a fitting choice given that the franchise was awarded on All Saints’ Day during a news conference at the Pontchartrain Hotel on St. Charles Avenue.

That December, oil and real estate businessman John W. Mecom Jr. purchased the franchise for $8.5 million. At 26, Mecom became the youngest owner in NFL history.

On Sept. 17, 1967, the Saints played their first regular-season game at Tulane Stadium. Eight years later, in August 1975, the Superdome became their permanent home.

For the next three decades, the Superdome became an integral part of Saints football and the culture surrounding the team.

Then came Hurricane Katrina.

In August 2005, Katrina devastated New Orleans and the Gulf Coast, flooding most of the city and severely damaging the Superdome. The disaster displaced hundreds of thousands of residents and forced the Saints from their home for the entire 2005 season.

With the Superdome unavailable, the Saints played their home games in San Antonio and Baton Rouge. Uncertainty surrounding the future of both the franchise and the city only compounded the challenges facing a community just beginning the long road to recovery.

One year later, the Saints finally returned home.

On Sept. 25, 2006, the Saints played their first game back in the Superdome, facing the Atlanta Falcons on Monday Night Football before a sold-out crowd of more than 70,000 fans.

Appropriately nicknamed “Domecoming,” the game became much more than a football game. It was a symbol of recovery and resilience.

Today marks 20 years since that unforgettable night inside the Superdome, when the Saints’ return reminded the world that New Orleans was still standing, still fighting and determined to come back stronger than ever.

The emotion inside the Superdome reached another level early in the first quarter when Steve Gleason blocked an Atlanta punt and Curtis Deloatch recovered in the end zone for the Saints’ first touchdown. The moment became one of the most iconic plays in franchise history.

That night, the Saints defeated the Falcons 23-3. They went on to finish the season 10-6 and advance to the NFC championship game for the first time in franchise history.

The Saints’ remarkable run ended with a loss to the Chicago Bears, but the 2006 season marked the beginning of a new era in New Orleans. More importantly, it reinforced a bond between a football team and its hometown that had been developing for nearly four decades.

As New Orleans rebuilt, so did the Saints.

Under new head coach Sean Payton and quarterback Drew Brees, a franchise that had spent much of its history searching for sustained success gave a community something to rally around each Sunday. The Saints became more than a source of entertainment. For many, they became a source of hope during one of the most difficult periods in the city’s history.

The journey that began with that emotional return to the Superdome in 2006 reached its defining moment three seasons later.

On Feb. 7, 2010, the Saints defeated the Indianapolis Colts 31-17 in Super Bowl XLIV, capturing the first championship in franchise history. For generations of Saints fans who had endured losing seasons, heartbreak and years when simply reaching the playoffs seemed impossible, the victory represented far more than a Lombardi Trophy.

New Orleans was finally a Super Bowl champion.

When the team returned home from Miami, thousands of fans filled the streets near the airport for an impromptu championship celebration that looked and felt like something only New Orleans could produce.

Over six decades, players, coaches and owners have changed. Tulane Stadium gave way to the Superdome. The paper bags of the “Aints” era were eventually replaced by division championships, playoff victories and a Super Bowl title.

But the connection between the Saints and New Orleans has remained.

It can be heard in the chants of “Who Dat?” and seen in the black and gold that fills the city on game days. It lives through generations of families who have passed down their Saints fandom and, in some cases, their season tickets from parents to children and grandchildren.

There have been unforgettable victories, devastating losses, seasons of hope and seasons fans would rather forget. Through it all, New Orleans has continued to embrace its football team.

Perhaps that is because the Saints and their city share something much deeper than geography.

Both know heartbreak. Both know the joy of celebration and the devastation of tragedy. And both have always found a way to come back.

Twenty years after the Saints came home to the Superdome and 60 years after Pete Rozelle announced that professional football was coming to New Orleans, that bond remains as much a part of the franchise as the fleur-de-lis on its helmet.

The Saints are part of New Orleans, and New Orleans is part of them.

item.title: Panthers vs Browns: Matchups to watch
item.description: Four matchups that should have a big impact on the result of the Carolina Panthers vs the Cleveland Browns.
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers bounced back from a big home loss to the Chicago Bears at home to notch a big win over the Atlanta Falcons on the road. They swept the matchups we highlighted in this space last week, particularly with the linebackers coming to play against Bijan Robinson (even though Robinson did manage a decent amount of rushing yards). Winning all the key matchups like that is an easy way to beat your opponent be 31 points. The Panthers will try to get a similar result in another road game, this time against the Cleveland Browns.

Jaelan Phillips vs Tytus Howard

The Browns traded for Howard in the offseason to try to solidify a leaky offensive line. He hasn’t provided a great return on that investment yet. The Browns as a team have yielded seven sacks through two weeks, and all but one of them has come from an edge rusher (shoutout former Panther A’Shawn Robinson for the other). A fair amount of that is on DeShaun Watson for holding the ball too long, but still, it’s an opportunity for Phillips to make it three straight games with a sack to start his tenure in Carolina. Howard has had some struggles in pass protection, so it’s a matchup the Panthers will be looking for Phillips to win. Howard has been decent in the run game, but he’s been just about the only Browns lineman that can boast that, and if Phillips can hold up there, the front should be able to keep the Browns woeful run game in check.

Jaycee Horn/Mike Jackson vs Denzel Boston

The safeties may have a role to play here as well, but the corners will get the bulk of the responsibility for covering the Browns rookie wide receiver. Boston has caught touchdown passes of over 40 yards in each of the first two games of the season. The Browns have not been good from play to play and drive to drive, so it’s paramount that the Panthers don’t let them off the hook with any big plays over the top. Now that it’s worked a couple of times, Watson will surely be hunting more deep looks to Boston in this one.

Panthers interior offensive line vs Mason Graham

The Browns have four sacks through two games. Two are from Mason Graham, and the other two are from safeties Grant Delpit and Ronnie Hickman. The rest of the Browns pass rush has been underwhelming so far (though there’s always a chance that Jared Verse wakes up). Based on the first two weeks, if the interior can hold up against Graham any blitzers from the secondary, the offensive line should be able to give Bryce Young time to find his targets.

Cleveland Browns fans vs DeShaun Watson

Browns fans have made it no secret that they’re not happy about their controversial quarterback getting paid tens of millions dollars per year to barely play and then play poorly when he does play. And Watson has not been shy about his frustration with people who are unhappy that he’s been a terrible quarterback while also allegedly being a terrible person. Shame on them, right? Well this will be Watson’s first regular season game in front of the home crowd. The Browns are coming off a win, and Watson played reasonably well in that win. It’ll be interesting to see if Browns fans will send more vitriol his way or if one decent performance in a win is enough to call off the dogs for the time being. Either way, if the Panthers defense can jump on Watson early and cause some poor offensive possessions, it’s very likely the crowd is going to turn on the home team and create a lot of strife.

item.title: Scouting the Enemy: Los Angeles Rams
item.description: The Denver Broncos host the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football. Here is a deeper look at their Week 3 opponent.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos host the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday Night Football. Both teams are coming off impressive Week 2 wins after faltering in their season openers. Here is a deeper look at the Broncos’ Week 3 opponent.

2025 Los Angeles Rams Season Review

The Rams finished their 2025 regular season with a 12-5 record earning second place in the NFC West. They would go on to lose the NFC Championship game to the Seattle Seahawks 31-27.

2026 Los Angeles Rams Offseason Additions and Departures

After failing to make the Super Bowl, General Manager Les Snead made a series of high-profile trades and moves this offseason. The big focus was on improving their defense.

They made a gargantuan trade with the Cleveland Browns to acquire Myles Garrett. However, he suffered a knee injury in Week 1 and won’t be available for their matchup versus the Broncos on Sunday Night Football. They also made a trade with the Kansas City Chiefs for star cornerback Trent McDuffie to improve their secondary.

Versatile defensive back Jaylen Watson was also added into the mix on a three-year deal. And the big surprise? Defensive lineman Aaron Donald came out of retirement to help the team’s pursuit of another Lombardi Trophy.

Instead of getting a player to help them win now in the 2026 NFL Draft, the Rams picked Alabama quarterback Ty Simpson in the first round. With Matthew Stafford getting up there in age, it’s understandable, but a lot of their fan base was certainly hoping for a player that could have provided a year one impact for the team.

In the second round, they took Ohio State tight end Max Klare—another curious decision since they brought back Tyler Higbee and had drafted Terrance Ferguson in the second round in the 2025 NFL Draft.

Offensive X-Factor: Quarterback Matthew Stafford

A handful of players could have earned this designation for the Rams. However, choosing last year’s MVP makes the most sense. That’s longtime quarterback Matthew Stafford who is in his eighteenth season in the NFL. Stafford’s productivity and longevity will certainly result in him eventually being enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Last season, Stafford threw for 4,707 yards and 46 touchdowns with just 8 interceptions. It was arguably one of the best seasons by a signal caller in NFL history. The Rams touted the best offense in the NFL in 2025.

His primary target last season was Puka Nacua, who reeled in 129 of 166 targets for 1,715 yards and 10 touchdowns. However, his availability for Sunday’s primetime matchup is uncertain and it seems unlikely he will be able to play.

Even so, Davante Adams gives them a top-notch wide receiver. Adams was the Rams’ second leading receiver with 60 receptions on 114 targets for 789 yards and 14 touchdowns last year. He is coming off a huge game versus the New York Giants where he had nearly 200 receiving yards and two touchdowns. The longtime veteran could be a huge problem for Denver.

There’s no doubt the Rams have a prolific passing attack with Stafford at the helm. He’s also been a hard quarterback to sack over the years. Dialing up the heat on Stafford and limiting Adams’ impact will be crucial for Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph. They can’t let their passing attack go wild on Sunday Night Football.

Defensive X-Factor: Cornerback Trent McDuffie

Myles Garrett certainly would have earned my designation here, but he won’t be playing. That’s good news for the Broncos. Aaron Donald earned some consideration, but I ultimately wound up going with two-time All-Pro cornerback Trent McDuffie.

The Rams gave up a lot of draft capital to acquire McDuffie and gave him one of the biggest contracts at the position in NFL history. In his first two games for the Rams, so far so good for the fifth-year cornerback. McDuffie has been targeted six times and allowed four receptions for just 23 yards. Against the Giants, he was able to pick off Jameis Winston after starting quarterback Jaxson Dart left the game due to injury.

Bo Nix already has a few bad decisions and turnovers this season. Denver can’t afford to have him get picked off by McDuffie in primetime. It’ll be interesting to see who McDuffie ends up trailing the most in coverage. Conventional wisdom says Courtland Sutton, but with the way the Broncos are trying to involve Jaylen Waddle in their aerial attack, it wouldn’t be surprising to see McDuffie matched up against Waddle on occasion.

How the Broncos can secure a victory over the Rams

ICYMI: I offered a blueprint for a Broncos’ victory yesterday. This is going to be a very tough game for Denver to win, but I do like the fact Denver will have homefield advantage. Some people will discount that, but the stadium was absolutely rocking due to fan noise against the Jaguars.

The Broncos need to have a strong rushing attack and have time consuming drives. This also means better execution on third down. The Rams have an offense that can strike quick and score a lot of points. This isn’t a game where I want to see Nix have to throw forty times and try and outduel Stafford.

I’d also like to see them do much better with starting field position. They did not do well in this regard against the Jaguars and were routinely inside their own fifteen-yard line to begin several drives. Hopefully Marvin Mims Jr. is able to return from injury and offer some impact as a returner on special teams.

And as I say most weeks—no more penalties. This is absolutely crippling the offense’s ability to be efficient. Somehow, someway, I think the Broncos will squeak out a victory in primetime.

Hart’s Prediction: Broncos 24, Rams 23.

item.title: Falcons – Packers recap: Awesome Atlanta gives Green Bay Grief
item.description: Atlanta finally puts a complete game together, and it’s enough to dominate Green Bay.
item.content:encoded:
Atlanta made a bunch of moves this offseason to turn over the roster, none of them designed to be franchise-altering. Instead, they looked to lift their floor, lock up the players they want around for the long term, and carefully avoided parting with too much draft capital or cap space in 2027. They wanted to walk the line between contending in 2026 and then making a splash next season, an admirable goal that hasn’t worked out well for these Falcons in the past several seasons.

Through two weeks, that gamble looked awful. Michael Penix Jr. had not returned, Tua Tagovailoa was injured, and Cooper Rush was submarining the offense. The line was struggling, the defense was gouged for a few big plays, A.J. Terrell got hurt, and the normally reliable Nick Folk was missing kicks. Had the Falcons lost on Thursday night against the Green Bay Packers, we would’ve been justified in declaring their hopes of contention in 2026 as unjustified and started resigning ourselves to daydreaming about 2027. After all, only seven 0-3 teams have ever made the playoffs.

But that’s not what happened. Instead, the Falcons few believed in got back the injured quarterback nearly everyone was criticizing and beat the hell out of the Packers. They started slow enough to make us concerned the same old Falcons were on the field, but after a 7-7 first quarter with a turnover and some puttering on offense and defense, Atlanta outscored Green Bay on Lambeau Field 28-7 the rest of the way. They turned Jordan Love into a pressure-pulped pumpkin. They turned Green Bay’s talented defense into a sieve. They held the Packers to the fewest rushing yards this franchise has ever allowed.

It was, as Mike Conti with 92.9 The Game noted, their largest margin of victory since 2019 against a struggling but still talented team that has had very recent success. The Falcons needed multiple things to click into place for this to be so lopsided, but for once a team that promised corrections actually delivered them, with the return of Penix proving to be decisive. All the talent and all the promise were on that football field working as a whole in a way we just haven’t seen consistently, and it’s a credit to this team from top to bottom that instead of sinking into the muck after their two losses, they’re now 1-2 and riding high.

I don’t know what to expect for 2026 now, both because the last three weeks have a been a roller coaster and because there have been such extreme lows and highs to consider. What I do know is that just showing the ability to do something like this is truly encouraging, and doing it on the road and under the lights with a quarterback just returning to game action after 10 months away from his last start is even more so. May they build, at long last, and let this be much more than one joyous game in a sea of mediocrity. Let 2026 be more than just a prelude to 2027, in the end, and the start of something special.

On to the full recap.

The Good

  • Bijan Robinson is heading toward an all-time great career. With Michael Penix Jr. wilting early, the Falcons got a break on a roughing the passer call and Bijan took over. He got one good block from Charlie Woerner, hit the sidelines, and then cut back inside and made multiple defenders miss before plowing through them to the five yard line for a 68 yard run. After one unproductive carry, he then then cut inside and jogged into the end zone for a score. Bijan was just warming up, too. After that, all he did was rush for another touchdown, a total of 194 yards, and chip in two grabs for 19 yards on top of that. It was an eye-popping day that threatens to become routine for the best running back in football, one where he made decisive cuts, bullied Packers defenders for extra yards, and seemed to know where lanes would be nanoseconds before they opened. He is a truly preposterous, special player.
  • Michael Penix Jr. got off to a slow start—more on that in the ugly section, because it was ugly—and was 1/5 with an interception at one point. After that, he went 17/20 for 250ish yards and a touchdown, showcasing impressive accuracy and getting the ball out incredibly quickly. Penix looked comfortable once he settled in doing just about anything asked of him and took a couple of big hits—including a roughing the passer—along the way. Penix was a slow starter at times before the injury and is still warming up, so we should expect some rough stretches going forward, but for most of the night he looked like the passer the Falcons invested so much in back in 2024. I’m very happy for him and, obviously, for all of us.
  • Brian Robinson Jr. has had to take over for a fan favorite in Tyler Allgeier, and to his credit he’s done extremely well. He looks decisive and rugged on returns after making a poor decision with the ball in Week 1 and has been an effective, physical runner who trusts his blocking. While Bijan obviously stole the headlines and absolutely dominated, Robinson 2 turned 10 carries into a tidy 50 yards and a touchdown. If he can keep rolling, this is the most dominant rushing attack in the NFL by a pretty wide margin.
  • Drake London was just waiting for someone to be able to get him the ball. After showing his frustration on the sideline last week, London got Penix back and immediately exploded for nearly 200 yards through the air, including a 68 yard catch-and-run where he absolutely annihilated rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse. He had nine catches for 194 yards in total and the Packers looked absolutely helpless trying to get him in open space or just cover him, which is exactly what you want to see from London. He’s a passionate player who very badly wants to win, and this had to feel extremely sweet.
  • Austin Hooper touchdown grabs? In 2026? I’ll take them. The Falcons have used Hooper more than I anticipated early, and Atlanta’s cast of playmakers take attention away from a player who is still a very capable receiver. With Kyle Pitts still not showing up in the box score—but throwing some nice blocks, we should note—Hooper has the opportunity to make his mark by being under the radar.
  • The oft-maligned offensive line had some rough stretches early but then found its footing in a major way. The Falcons focused on getting the ball out quickly to mitigate some of their pass protection issues, but they largely kept Penix clean and bullied Green Bay’s defensive front on runs all night. It was great to see.
  • Tommy Rees should get his flowers for working Penix into a rhythm and relentlessly attacking Green Bay’s weaknesses all night. We’ve complained long and bitterly in recent years about the way Dirk Koetter, Arthur Smith, and Zac Robinson, for all their individual strengths as play callers, seemed hellbent on doing things their way regardless of personnel and opponent; Rees took a quarterback returning from his third ACL injury and dialed up a plan that got the ball out, attacked the middle of the field in a way I don’t think Green Bay expected, and took advantage of his absurd arm talent. He’ll need to stack these games, obviously, but I do think poor Cooper Rush was just that limited.
  • This team lost multiple defenders up front and they haven’t slowed down at all. Brandon Dorlus and Gervon Dexter had this overmatched Packers defensive line in hell, which in turn caused Jordan Love endless trouble. Dorlus just kept throwing Love badly off balance and Dexter was pushing Packers into Love’s lap, and while this whole rotation has fared well, these two guys have the potential to be one of the most imposing interior pass rush duos in the league. Dorlus is, for my money, already one of the most underrated defensive linemen going.
  • Divine Deablo’s big hit on a scrambling Jordan Love for a loss was a thing of beauty. Pair that with some really nice work in coverage and you got a stew going, baby.
  • Kendal Daniels was everywhere, showcasing the physicality and instincts that made me believe in him in the first place. I predicted that he’d start but thought there would be early hiccups to go with that; so far, I’ve seen almost nothing but good things.
  • Cameron Thomas looks like one of the more impactful additions of the offseason already, with the team’s sole sack of the night despite all their pressure, and that’s the third straight week where he’s been a solid run defender while bringing the heat.
  • Billy Bowman Jr.’s pass breakup was just stellar timing and awareness from a player who had been out a long time and could’ve been rusty, but was not.
  • C.J. Henderson had a big job stepping in for A.J. Terrell, but he was up to the task. He had multiple nice plays and tight coverage throughout the first half, showcasing the talent that made him a first round pick in the first place before his career stagnated. In Atlanta, he’s taking to this defense extremely well and showing great instincts and the ability to impact plays, and I have a lot of confidence in his ability to hold up while Terrell is out.
  • Zach Harrison was a surprise cut who then came back on the practice squad, and now is finally back on the Falcons roster where he belongs. He reminded us of that in the second quarter of this one, when he went way up to block Trey Smack’s field goal attempt that would’ve tied the game. It was great to see him making such a big play, and he was impactful on defense as well.
  • Xavier Watts nearly picked off Jordan Love’s shot to the end zone late in the fourth quarter, and then turned around and did pick him off by jumping the route on Love’s final pass of the game. The bonafide playmaker has been good to start the 2026 season but hadn’t had any big plays yet, and hopefully this gets him going so he can pick off Tyler Shough, too.
  • The defense really carried its weight in this one. Over and over again, they got timely pressure on Jordan Love to force a panicky throw, punished the Packers for daring to run behind their leaky line, and broke up deep passing attempts that would’ve gone for major gains. The run defense has been particularly impressive this year, defying our expectations, and absolutely smothered Green Bay all evening in that regard. Give these players a ton of credit, but also kudos to a coaching staff that has a ton of confidence and had a tremendous plan for this Green Bay offense.
  • Nick Folk looked like he was back and settled in, hitting his two field goal tries with a minimum of fuss and no worrying leans to the left or right.

The Ugly

  • We knew Michael Penix Jr. would be a little rusty, but he was more than a little rusty to start this one. His interception on the first drive was a can’t-throw-that shot over the middle right to the defender, and he repeatedly missed on Atlanta’s initial drives while looking panicky. The intentional grounding call nearly killed Atlanta’s first scoring drive before a fortunate roughing the passer revived it, and it looked like Penix was heading for a rough night. Happily, he was not.
  • When the offense is cooking like this, it doesn’t matter that Kyle Pitts was lightly targeted again; I’m sure he’d tell you that himself. I do think there will be weeks in the near future when Bijan is slightly less productive and teams focus on taking London out of the game, and that’s when the Falcons will have to figure out how to get Pitts the ball so he can shine. We know the ability’s there, but I’m still waiting for the team to utilize an impactful playmaker more frequently, which is the smallest possible sour note in a game like this.
  • Mike Hughes is still a willing tackler who has long stretches of competence in coverage, but he’s been losing too many battles in coverage thus far in 2026. I believe he was on the receiving end of both Packers touchdown passes and found himself out of position on both, though I’ll caution that’s just based off snap reactions to the broadcast. If he can’t rebound in the weeks ahead before A.J. Terrell returns, it’s very possible he’ll be out of a starting job with Billy Bowman Jr. back and Avieon Terrell coming on. He does have time to right the ship, however.
  • We’ll have to see what’s going on with Jessie Bates, who was injured last night but did return. As Joe Patrick noted, Bates missed a lot of work this summer and has not looked like himself to start the year, with some coverage miscues and decisions that have left players like Hughes on an island unexpectedly. We’ll hope he’s fully healthy by the time Week 4 rolls around and can keep knocking rust off.
  • It won’t be quite this fun every week. Bummer.

The Wrapup

Game MVP

Many worthy candidates in this one, but of course it’s Bijan Robinson after he scored two of Atlanta’s touchdowns, ripped off nearly 200 yards on the ground, and dominated and demoralized Green Bay. First of several this year, I’d wager.

One Takeaway

This may well be a high variance team that flips from thrilling to frustrating, but they are capable of putting together a performance like this. The fact that it happened as Penix returned to the field bodes well for them hitting that potential more often.

Next Week

The hated, smelly Saints in primetime. That should be a fun one.

Final Word

Greatgame.

item.title: Washington Commanders vs Seattle Seahawks Week 3: Five Questions with Field Gulls
item.description: Will Washington be able to turn things around against last year’s Super Bowl champions?
item.content:encoded:
It’s week 3 of the NFL season, and the 0-2 Washington Commanders will be facing a 2-0 Seattle Seahawks team at home in Northwest Stadium in Landover, MD this Sunday at 1:00 p.m. ET. Despite losing starting QB Sam Darnold to a glute injury on the first drive of the first game, the Seahawks have managed to beat the Patriots 13-10 in week 1 and beat the Cardinals 31-7 in week 2. It is unclear if Darnold will return to play in week 3, but he has practiced this week.

On offense, the Seahawks are coached by OC Brian Fleury, former TEs coach and run-game coordinator of the 49ers from 2022 to 2025. A TEs coach has good insight into both the blocking and pass-catching aspects of offense due to TEs being heavily involved in both duties. The fact that Fleury was also the run-game coordinator for the 49ers means he should be well suited to understanding and coaching all aspects of the Shanahan offense (note that Cowboys OC Klayton Adams was formerly a TEs coach for the Colts and OL coach for the Cardinals who designed their prolific run game before moving to Dallas). So far, the Seahawks offense has stayed true to its Shanahan roots, with heavy use of under center, play action passing, and an outside-zone run game. Perhaps to simplify the passing game for a backup QB, the Seahawks have been targeting WR Jaxon Smith-Njigba with an absurd 44% share of targets (last year he led the NFL with a 35.8% target share). It makes sense to simplify things for your backup QB by scheming him to just throw it to his best player.

On defense, the Seahawks are still coached by head coach Mike Macdonald, former DC of the Ravens, and DC Aden Durde, former defensive line coach of the Cowboys. Perhaps unsurprising given that their DC is a former DL coach, the Seahawks defense is anchored around the excellent play of their defensive line. Last year, the Seahawks were able to achieve the 6th-best QB pressure rate despite the 7th-lowest blitz rate, meaning they were able to get pressure rushing four most of the time, and leave more players back in coverage to stop passing plays and explosive plays. The result is a defense that allows the NFL’s fewest passing yards and 9th-fewest rushing yards through two games this year.

I asked John Gilbert of Field Gulls five questions to better understand the state of the Seahawks and what to look for in this game.

1) The Seahawks defense has held their opponents to 10 or fewer points in the last two games. How much of this is personnel, how much is scheme, and what is special about Mike Macdonald’s scheme and playcalling?

Holding both 2026 opponents they have faced to 10 or fewer points really seems to be a continuation of how the Seattle defense finished the 2025 season, which was by holding five of the last nine teams played to 10 or fewer points. Of the games in which the other team has managed to put more than ten points on the board against this defense since Thanksgiving, they were quarterbacked by Philip Rivers (16), Matthew Stafford (37 & 27) and Drake Maye (13), and any team with a quarterback that isn’t in the tier of those named has struggled against the defense. 

As for what makes Macdonald’s defense so successful, it’s not one thing in particular. The players are good, but Macdonald makes them better by putting them in a position to succeed by understanding the tendencies of the opponent, while simultaneously giving his players the freedom to operate as needed for success. For example, former undrafted free agent linebacker Drake Thomas changed the defensive front Macdonald had called on a key second and one near midfield early in the game against the Cardinals. Similarly, on the fourth down that effectively clinched the NFC Championship for the Seahawks, DeMarcus Lawrence recognized what the Rams were trying to do and broke off his assignment to prevent Stafford having an easy completion to Kyren Williams for either a first down or score. It’s a rare combination of a scheme that confuses opponents, with players who perform at a high level within the system and have the skills and football IQ to operate with a higher level of freedom, and the experience necessary in the system to play fast without having to think to analyze how to react. 

2) On the other side of the ball, how has the Seahawks offense looked? Is it different under new OC Brian Fleury and what changes with Drew Lock vs Sam Darnold at QB?

The season opener did not start off well for anyone hoping for the offense would be as explosive as it was last season, as the team was shutout by the Patriots until after halftime. Certainly a part of that is likely due to the fact that Sam Darnold’s injury meant Drew Lock taking over, as well as some rust overall as the starters had not played during the preseason. 

The fact that the backup is in at quarterback means the jury is largely still out as far as a lot of the questions that surrounded the offense heading into the season. 

With that said, through the first two games one of the consistent threads that has continued through from 2025 has been the continued usage of two and three tight end packages. Specifically, during the 2025 season the Seahawks used 12- or 13-personnel on a little more than a third of their offensive snaps, while so far in 2026 the usage has been even higher. A big piece of that, of course, is likely that they were up big and running the ball a lot against the Cardinals in the second half of Week 2, so it remains to be seen how much they’ll rely on their tight end heavy packages in more competitive contests. 

In addition, Fleury has tweaked how the Seattle offense uses motion through the first two games, and that has made things more difficult for opponents to figure out what’s coming.


3) What is your overall opinion of Seahawks GM John Schneider and has it evolved since the hiring of Mike Macdonald? Did you ever think he should have been sent packing along with Pete Carroll for a completely fresh start?


After coming out of the gates on an absolute scorcher and drafting multiple Hall of Fame caliber players to start his career as a general manager, things went off the rails for several years. From 2017 through 2021 the results of the team’s drafting was not on par with what is necessary for sustained success in the NFL, and that certainly contributed to Carroll’s demise. A big piece of the issues from 2018 on appear to have been reworking the draft board and an over reliance on looking for “maturity” in the wake of the Malik McDowell debacle of 2017. Beginning in 2018 the Seahawks draft classes were consistently among the oldest in the NFL, while many of their biggest hits to come out of those drafts were players like DK Metcalf who were among the younger members of their respective draft class. 

Where the wheels truly came off, though, was when the Seahawks made a conscious decision to effectively punt on the 2021 draft as a result of the anticipated uncertainty of the COVID season. Seattle made only three selections in the 2021 draft after trading a first and a third for Jamal Adams, a fifth for Gabe Jackson and a seventh for Carlos Dunlap. Of course, the draft is about uncertainty, and the Loser’s Curse is a concept developed decades ago regarding the uncertainty of the draft. 

That all said, since 2022 Schneider has been back on a heater, and the quality of the roster shows. Even after the departure in free agency of Kenneth Walker, Coby Bryant, Boye Mafe and Tariq Woolen, the team is stacked and Schneider has secured his place with the team for years to come, in spite of many calls (including my own) for the team to move on when it moved on from Carroll. 


4) Who is one Seahawks player on offense and one player on defense that Washington fans probably don’t know much about, but should?

The aforementioned Drake Thomas on defense is a player Commanders fans may not know, but he will seemingly be everywhere on defense against both the run and in coverage. Thomas came to Seattle as a waiver claim in 2023 during Carroll’s final season, and laid claim to a starting spot at linebacker in 2025, and at this point there appears to be no looking back. 

On offense, Commanders fans certainly know JSN, and Tory Horton’s performance against the Commanders during the 2025 season may be etched into the memory of many Washington fans, but A.J. Barner is the name to watch out for. The third-year tight end is a monster as a blocker, and dangerous enough as a receiving threat that the coaches aren’t hesitant to call his number during high leverage situations. 

5) How should Washington go about gameplanning this matchup on both sides of the ball?

In the past, the way to gameplan when facing Drew Lock has been to sit back and wait for Lock to make a mistake, but so far this year he has played largely mistake-free football. That makes it likely that the best way to slow down the offense is to focus on stopping the run enough on early downs that Lock is forced to make plays on third and long, which might eventually lead to turnovers or punts. However, so far this season, Lock has not hesitated to push the easy button and just throw it to JSN, so Washington will need to stop, or at least slow down, JSN in order to have a shot. 

On the other side of the ball, the defense can be attacked, but it has been savvy veterans or young gunslingers who have found success against Macdonald’s defense, and that’s not how most fans and observers would describe Mariota, so it may be as simple as relying on Mariota to freelance and make things happen with his legs in order for the Commanders to stay in the game. 

A companion article to this with my answers to John’s questions will be linked here when it is available.

Thanks again to John Gilbert for taking time out of his day to answer our questions about the Seahawks.

item.title: Giants vs. Titans: Can the Giants’ offense rebound on a short week?
item.description: What will the Giants offense look like with Jameis Winston at QB against the Tennessee Titans defense?
item.content:encoded:
It was a long flight home to the Meadowlands for the New York Giants after their Monday nightmare against the Los Angeles Rams.

That flight turned into a long and trying Tuesday as the Giants learned that starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost for the remainder of the season. In doing so, the keys to the Giants’ offense were passed to backup quarterback Jameis Winston.

Winston’s first test will come against the Tennessee Titans and a collection of former faces. This game had been circled for a while, largely because of all the storylines surrounding it. Brian Daboll, cornerback Cor’Dale Flott, wide receiver Wan’Dale Robinson, center Austin Schlottman, and tight end Daniel Bellinger are all familiar familiar with Winston, as well as many of their offensive linemen, tight ends, and running backs.

Robert Saleh will be calling the Titans’ defense, but he has plenty of resources from whom he can seek insight.

The Titans were expected to be a relatively easy win after the Giants steamrolled the Dallas Cowboys. Now, the Giants are only slim favorites at home. How will the offense respond in Winston’s first test?

Jameis Winston at QB

The Giants had to adapt to a new reality early on in their loss to the Rams, when Dart was lost for the game to a knee injury.

It didn’t go well and Winston appeared rattled when he came on the field for the Giants against the Rams. While his job as the veteran backup is to be a steady presence in troubled times, he did not appear comfortable at all on Monday night. Winston appeared to distrust his protection, not see the defense well, nor throw the ball well.

For as bad as Winston looked after coming onto the field following Dart’s injury, there is the silver lining that the Titans can’t be sure just what the Giants’ offense will look like with a pure pocket passer under center. They can be sure that Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely will still be centerpieces, but they can’t know just what form the offense will take.

Winston is a different type of quarterback from Dart. The two share charisma and competitiveness, as well as a baseball background and impressive arm talent, however they’re very different athletes. That’s going to change how the Giants structure and call their offense. The quarterback run game that kept defenses honest is gone, as is the threat of a scramble once things break down.

However, Winston is also a much more experienced quarterback who has seen just about every type of defense the NFL has to offer, and is willing to attack them all. That can get him into trouble, but it can also be an asset if the Giants embrace it. It’s worth remembering that the Winston-led Giants never trailed in regulation against the Lions and he was solid against the Green Bay Packers, and that was with a more flawed coaching staff and a worse offensive roster.

Winston has the arm strength to push the ball down the field and the Giants have enough pieces to take advantage of mistakes in coverage when they happen — assuming Winston can control his characteristic aggression long enough for them to manifest. The possibility of explosive passing plays could also loosen things up for the run game, which we know John Harbaugh wants to rely upon.

The Giants have very limited time in which to shift gears from Dart to Winston, but the fact that the Titans can’t know exactly what the Giants will do is an advantage they should seize.

How will the Titans defend Jameis?

The Giants aren’t the only ones who have to shift gears after the injury to Dart. The Titans now have a very different quarterback to defend, with different challenges.

Conventional wisdom suggests that the Titans will focus on Harbaugh and Greg Roman’s desire to be a run-first team. It would follow that they would focus on stacking the box and force Winston to beat them through the air.

However, Saleh is (yet another) member of the Fangio tree. He prefers to rotate between Cover 4 and Cover 3 looks, and San Francisco ran among the highest rates of those coverages in the NFL. Saleh’s defense was also among the League leaders in nickel usage. The Titans obviously don’t have the same defensive personnel as the 49er’s, nor do they have anything like San Francisco’s offense. However, Saleh’s overall philosophy has been pretty consistent over the years.

The Fangio style of defense is designed to both prevent explosive plays and confuse quarterbacks with late rotations.

The Titans won’t have to worry about the Giants’ quarterback run game with Winston under center, nor will they have to pay particular attention to spying a mobile quarterback.

The Giants should be alert to the possibility that rather than try to go against their defensive philosophy to sell out to defend the run, they’ll instead try to force Jameis Winston to be patient and frustrate him.

Winston has a bad history of throwing the ball to the team wearing the wrong color jerseys, and safety Amani Hooker intercepted Jalen Hurts twice last week (nearly returning one for a touchdown). The Giants could look to be a more explosive passing offense with Winston, moving away from the surgical attack they used with Dart to emphasize Winston’s arm strength and aggressiveness. Playing coverage would keep a lid on the Giants’ offense and potentially take away Winston’s biggest asset, while also providing the defense with opportunities to take the ball away.

Inside, the Titans would be counting on defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to both pressure Winston into making a mistake as well as disrupting runs behind the line of scrimmage. Their linebackers played relatively well against the Philadelphia Eagles last week, and could frustrate the Giants’ underneath passing game.

Attacking Saleh’s defense

How the Giants attack the Titans’ defense will likely be decided over the first drive or two and there will likely be a “feeling out” period for both of these teams.

The Giants are shifting gears in an offense that’s still new. There’s little tape on the Giants’ offense and basically none on the Giants’ offense with Winston. On the flip side, the Titans are only playing their third game in a new defense. While Saleh’s general scheme and philosophy, there’s still only limited tape on how it’s being applied to the Titans’ roster.

The easy answer is that the Giants should counter-punch however the Titans opt to defend them. If the Titans try to lock down the run, the Giants should take the dare to beat them through the air. Conversely, if the Titans play coverage, the Giants should play to their running strengths and use an intermediate passing attack to supplement the run and attack the voids underneath the deep coverage zones. That may be frustrating for Winston, but keeping the offense moving would (hopefully) mitigate that until opportunities for explosive plays open up.

The Giants’ offense wants to be based on running the ball, however they do have an unconventionally built roster.

The Giants are heavy on running backs and tight ends, but light on receivers. If the Giants play a more conventional passing offense, they’ll be able to use their personnel to disguise their intentions. Isaiah Likely and Theo Johnson are both athletic tight ends who can stress the seams of Saleh’s Cover 3 shells, while all of the Giants’ running backs are able to catch the ball. Likewise, Nabers, Darnell Mooney, and Likely are all able to pick up yards after catch on screens or quick passes to the flats.

The Giants’ lives were made significantly more difficult on offense after the injury to Dart. That, however, doesn’t mean that it’s time to pack it in. They still have weapons and pieces that can allow them to continue to win. The job of Harbaugh, his coaching staff, and Winston is now to steady the ship and rally the team with a win at home.

item.title: Colts just proved why the NFL stands for the “No Fun League”
item.description: The Colts caught the NFL in the most hypocritical stance ever.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL loves money. They do anything and everything to get as much of it as possible. Stream the season on 29 different platforms? No problem. Span the globe and play in 10 different countries? You bet. They love it so much that they are willing to fine players like Indianapolis Colts’ Matt Goncalves $9K for his celebration against the Chiefs. It’s a matter that is out of hand. 

What was Goncalves’ offense? Surely he must have gestured towards the other team in a crude manner, or maybe he inappropriately engaged fans on the sideline. Nope. After receiving the ball on a Tyler Warren touchdown, Goncalves acted like he was taking a drink. It was labeled as an “offensive demonstration”.

Mind you, this is the same league that promotes adult beverages every five seconds on their commercial breaks. The same league that has official tailgate and pregame areas sponsored by these brands. A league that sells a copious amount in the stadium and has designated areas in the stadium named after these companies has the gall to call this offensive. If the ad running on your television during an NFL game isn’t for an adult beverage, it’s for a betting site. If the ad isn’t for a betting site, it’s for an adult beverage. 

Taunting and lewd gestures towards other players and fans are acceptable as fineable offenses. Heck, even fining players $9K like the league did Goncalves is ok too, if the NFL is willing to uproot its current business model. This type of culture has permeated the NFL so much that I wouldn’t have been surprised to see that celebration officially sponsored by one of these companies. That’s how often fans are hit with it. 

The “No Fun League” strikes again. Young, impressionable children can’t see that type of celebration on television while their parent is building a can tower next to them on the table during the broadcast. They are blasted on repeat by ads and in person sponsorships, but when a player chugs a drink, which could have been literally anything, that is a step too far. Give me a break.

item.title: Cowboys news: Dallas secondary depth will be tested vs Ravens
item.description: Here is today’s Dallas Cowboys news.
item.content:encoded:
After a much needed bounce back win in week two, the Dallas Cowboys are set to take on the Baltimore Ravens in Rio for their week three matchup against the 1-1 Ravens.

Both teams are heading into Rio a bit banged up, with some questionable field conditions on the horizon.
